title: Rose-derived extracellular vesicle-like particles enable anti-melanogenesis by suppressing the key melanogenic pathway in skin cells.
authors: Zhou, Sirui; Li, Huijing; Yang, Ying; Zeng, Weiying; Li, Dongxiao; Qiu, Tianxin; Lu, Weiguo; Zhao, Kewei
journal: Extracellular vesicles and circulating nucleic acids
abstract: Aim: Abnormal skin pigmentation is not merely a common cosmetic concern but is also associated with pigmentation disorders and an elevated risk of malignant lesions such as melanoma. To overcome the adverse effects of existing antimelanogenic agents, we developed rose-derived extracellular vesicle-like particles (RS-EVLP) as a novel and biocompatible melanogenesis inhibitor. Methods: RS-EVLP were isolated from roses and characterized by transmission electron microscopy and mass spectrometry. Their anti-melanogenic effects were evaluated in B16 cells via melanin content and tyrosinase activity assays. Molecular mechanisms were investigated using molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, and surface plasmon resonance (SPR) analysis. In vivo efficacy was assessed in a zebrafish model, followed by a clinical trial in human volunteers. Results: RS-EVLP exhibited a bilayer nanostructure (50-150 nm) and contained natural anti-melanogenic components, including luteolin and procyanidin B3. They showed high binding affinity to microphthalmia-associated transcription factor (MITF) and tyrosinase-related protein 1 (TRP-1). In B16 cells, RS-EVLP dose-dependently reduced melanin content and tyrosinase activity by downregulating MITF and the transcription of tyrosinase (TYR)/TRP-1/TRP-2 enzyme system. In zebrafish, RS-EVLP reduced melanin spot area by 24% +/- 17.5%. Clinical studies confirmed that a 5% RS-EVLP formulation progressively enhanced skin brightness as skin penetration efficiency increased. Conclusion: RS-EVLP overcomes the limitations in bioavailability and toxicity associated with traditional synthetic whitening agents, offering a promising natural alternative for developing whitening cosmeceuticals.

title: Transcription factor-driven metabolic stratification reveals glycolytic and lipogenic subtypes with distinct prognostic and functional features in pancreatic cancer.
authors: Ke, Jie; Liu, Shuai; Xu, Junming; Wu, Fenfang
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) exhibits profound molecular and metabolic heterogeneity associated with distinct phenotypic states. However, the contribution of transcription factor (TF)-driven regulatory programs to metabolic subtype stratification remains poorly understood. This study aims to determine whether TF-based classification can identify prognostically relevant glycolytic and lipogenic PDAC subtypes. METHODS: Bulk transcriptomic data from multiple PDAC cohorts and single-cell RNA sequencing data were integrated to characterize TF-associated metabolic heterogeneity. Metabolic signatures and TFs were quantified using single-sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA) and AddModule Score (AMS). Differential expression, enrichment analysis, integrative bulk and single-cell transcriptomic analysis, and deep neural network-based metabolic flux modeling were performed to investigate metabolic programs and functional differences between TF-defined subtypes. Additionally, RNA interference, RT-qPCR, lipid droplets staining, lactate assay, and transwell assays were used to evaluate the roles of TP63 in metabolic regulation. RESULTS: Glycolytic and lipogenic TF-defined metabolic subtypes were identified across multiple independent PDAC cohorts. These subtypes exhibited distinct metabolic programs, differentiation states, and prognostic outcomes. The glycolytic TF-defined subtype was associated with worse prognosis and differentiation, whereas the lipogenic TF-defined subtype exhibited more favorable clinical features. Integration of public bulk and single-cell transcriptomic analyses, together with deep neural network-based metabolic flux modeling, revealed consistent metabolic heterogeneity at both cellular and functional levels. Notably, TP63 was identified as a potential regulator of glycolytic-lipogenic metabolic reprogramming in PDAC. CONCLUSIONS: TF-based classification delineates glycolytic and lipogenic subtypes in PDAC, underscoring the critical role of TF-regulated metabolic programs in patient stratification. These findings highlight the prognostic significance of glycolytic and lipogenic metabolic heterogeneity and support the development of metabolism-targeted therapeutic strategies.

title: Population-specific transcriptomic shifts underlie secondary metabolic diversification in Aspergillus flavus Link and the domestication of Aspergillus oryzae (Ahlb.).
authors: Drott, Milton T; Wang, Yen-Wen; Hatmaker, E Anne; Mercado-Soto, Nayanna M; Elmore, J Mitch; Luciano-Rosaro, Dianiris; Yu, Jae-Hyuk; Rokas, Antonis; Gibbons, John G; Huttenlocher, Anna; Yang, Kunlong; Keller, Nancy P
abstract: The genomic signatures of microbial domestication remain poorly understood within the context of natural population variation. Here, we demonstrate that Aspergillus oryzae, the filamentous fungus used in soy sauce and sake production, shares more recent ancestry with a predominantly northern, largely non-aflatoxigenic population of Aspergillus flavus (population C). A. oryzae isolates also overlap with the recently described, clinically enriched A. flavus population D, suggesting multiple domestication events. All isolates tested retained pathogenicity in a zebrafish infection model. At the transcriptomic level, populations are significantly differentiated and respond differently to spore density, suggesting population-specific adaptations to ecological conditions. Although most transcriptomic variation was consistent with phylogenetic relationships, several co-expression modules exhibited significantly greater divergence than expected from phylogeny alone, suggesting that phenotypic diversification may sometimes occur through the reorganization of transcriptomic architectures. A. oryzae also displayed elevated expression of a carbohydrate-metabolism module; however, this pattern was consistent with phylogenetic differentiation, suggesting that enhanced carbohydrate metabolism may have begun evolving prior to domestication or may be most apparent under fermentation-relevant conditions. Population-specific variation is also evident among secondary metabolite (SM) gene clusters. While A. oryzae shows markedly reduced expression of aflatoxin biosynthesis genes, this trend does not extend across the entire secondary metabolome. Using machine-learning-based gene regulatory network inference, we identified population-specific transcriptomic differences linked to distinct transcription factors, with evidence for both cis- and trans-acting regulatory divergence, but no changes in global regulators such as laeA. Together, these findings provide new insights into the domestication of A. oryzae, its global significance, and the microevolution of fungal secondary metabolic pathways.

title: Integrated multi-omics and experimental analyses identify JUNB as a candidate biomarker associated with immune-related processes in psoriasis.
authors: Zhang, Jiayin; Shi, Jiaqi; Zhong, Mi
abstract: INTODUCTION: Psoriasis is an immune-mediated inflammatory skin disease involving abnormal keratinocyte activation and immune infiltration, while the key transcriptional regulators underlying epidermal-immune interactions remain insufficiently defined. AIM: To identify and validate core immune-related biomarkers linked to psoriasis pathogenesis, emphasising transcription factor JUNB, through integrated bioinformatics and experimental approaches. MATERIAL AND METHODS: Bulk transcriptome datasets (GSE14905, GSE66511, GSE154200) were examined to detect differentially expressed genes (DEGs), while three ML approaches (LASSO, random forest, and XGBoost) were used to identify hub genes. Diagnostic performance was evaluated via ROC curves. Immune infiltration patterns were assessed using CIBERSORT. Single-cell RNA-seq (GSE162183) was used for cellular localization. In vitro experiments were conducted in HaCaT cells stimulated with IL-17A, with JUNB knockdown via siRNA, and expression levels of IL-6, IL-22, and IFNG measured by qRT-PCR. RESULTS: JUNB and S100A7 were consistently upregulated in psoriasis across datasets and showed good diagnostic performance (AUC > 0.85). Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) demonstrated JUNB to be enriched in IL-17, NF-kappaB, and TNF signalling pathways. Immune analysis indicated JUNB was positively correlated with neutrophils and macrophages. Single-cell analysis confirmed JUNB and S100A7 were primarily expressed in keratinocytes. In vitro, IL-17A stimulation was associated with increased JUNB and S100A7 expression, while JUNB knockdown significantly reduced downstream inflammatory cytokines. CONCLUSIONS: These findings indicate that JUNB is closely associated with IL-17-related inflammatory responses and immune infiltration in psoriasis, providing mechanistic context for its involvement in disease pathogenesis and supporting its potential utility as a diagnostic biomarker.

title: A cytoplasmic cis-acting circuit confines PI3K/AKT-driven lineage plasticity in bladder cancer.
authors: Dong, Xuan; Li, Yutong; Yan, Yongtai; Xiong, Hong; Wu, Pulin; Chen, Yongjie; Yi, Zhaofeng; Zhou, Cong; Zuo, Ling; Liu, Hongwei
abstract: Bladder cancer (BCa) is a prevalent urological malignancy characterized by high recurrence rates and limited therapeutic options for advanced disease. Circular RNAs (circRNAs) have emerged as critical regulators of gene expression in cancer, yet their roles in BCa progression remain incompletely understood. Here, circ_0006845 (circNFAT5) is identified as a tumor-suppressive circRNA that is significantly downregulated in BCa tissues and cell lines. Functional assays demonstrate that circNFAT5 inhibits BCa cell proliferation, migration, and invasion in vitro and suppresses subcutaneous tumor growth in vivo. Mechanistically, circNFAT5 localizes predominantly to the cytoplasm and functions as a competing endogenous RNA (ceRNA) by competitively sponging miR-552-3p, thereby relieving post-transcriptional repression of the Forkhead box O1 (FoxO1) transcription factor. Single-cell RNA sequencing analysis further identifies Ubiquitin C (UBC) as a potential downstream target of FoxO1, with FoxO1 occupancy at the UBC promoter supported by ChIP-seq and computational docking predicting a potential interaction. Intercellular communication profiling identifies ANNEXIN, COMPLEMENT, SEMA3, VEGF, and VISFATIN as dominant PI3K/AKT-associated axis mediating cross-talk between FoxO1-low tumor subpopulations and stromal cells within the tumor microenvironment. Drug sensitivity analysis predicts that FoxO1-low BCa cells may exhibit enhanced sensitivity to cisplatin, gemcitabine, and PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway inhibitors. These findings delineate a circNFAT5/miR-552-3p/FoxO1/UBC regulatory axis associated with PI3K/AKT signaling that may contribute to BCa progression, nominating FoxO1 as a candidate prognostic biomarker and a potential therapeutic stratification marker.

title: Low-dose Juglone Attenuates Pressure Overload-Induced Cardiac Hypertrophy through Lys207-dependent FoxO1 activation and Mitochondrial protection.
authors: Chen, Hongyu; Yang, Zhihao; Zhang, Cheng; Ge, Chengxin; Zhao, Yingliang; Cheng, Shaopeng; Wang, Yilin; Chen, Hao; Xu, Can; Wang, Dongjin; Yang, Jie
abstract: Pressure overload-induced cardiac hypertrophy is characterized by mitochondrial dysfunction and redox imbalance. Here, we investigated the efficacy, safety window, and redox-regulatory mechanism of juglone, a naturally occurring 5-hydroxy-1,4-naphthoquinone. In mice subjected to transverse aortic constriction (TAC), high-dose juglone induced cardiac, hepatic, and renal toxicity, whereas 1mg/kg/day was well tolerated and attenuated cardiac hypertrophy. Juglone also suppressed Ang II-induced cardiomyocyte hypertrophy in vitro and preserved mitochondrial ultrastructure and mitochondrial membrane potential, respiration, ATP production, and redox homeostasis. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) revealed that juglone reduced stress-associated cardiomyocyte states and enriched calcium-handling cardiomyocytes. Integrated transcriptomic analyses, Biotin-Juglone pull-down assay, surface plasmon resonance, cellular thermal shift assays, molecular docking, and mutational analyses identified FoxO1 as a functional target of juglone. Juglone engaged the FoxO1 DNA-binding domain in a Lys207-dependent manner, and was associated with FoxO1 deacetylation, nuclear accumulation, and transcriptional activation. Activated FoxO1 induced Sesn3 transcription and restored AMPK phosphorylation at Thr172. Sesn3 silencing markedly attenuated juglone-induced AMPK activation and impaired its protective effects against cardiomyocyte hypertrophy and mitochondrial dysfunction. FoxO1 silencing, FoxO1-K207Q mutation, blockade of FoxO1 deacetylation, or inhibition of FoxO1 transcriptional activity impaired these benefits. Importantly, myocardium from patients with aortic valve stenosis-associated hypertrophy exhibited increased FoxO1 acetylation, reduced cardiomyocyte nuclear FoxO1 localization, decreased Sesn3 expression and AMPK phosphorylation, and increased 4-HNE. Collectively, low-dose juglone attenuates pathological hypertrophy and preserves mitochondrial homeostasis through the FoxO1-Sesn3-AMPK axis, while highlighting the importance of dose-dependent redox effects in determining its therapeutic efficacy and systemic toxicity.

title: Phosphorylation by CaMKIV regulates the transcriptional repressor activity and half-life of REST/NRSF.
authors: Tsushima Semini, Hanako; Corradi, Beatrice; Canevari, Caterina; Shmal, Dmytro; Chiacchiaretta, Martina; Liessi, Nara; Di Fonzo, Andrea; Carminati, Emanuele; Armirotti, Andrea; Fassio, Anna; Maragliano, Luca; Rocchi, Anna; Benfenati, Fabio
abstract: Repressor Element-1 (RE1)-Silencing Transcription Factor (REST) homeostatically regulates neural activity by repressing a large cluster of neural genes. However, whether REST can be regulated by calcium(2+) (Ca(2+))-activated kinases is unknown. We investigated Ca(2+)/calmodulin-dependent protein kinases (CaMKs) as upstream regulators of REST fate and activity. We show that REST is phosphorylated by CaMKIV at Ser(322) site in the fifth-to-sixth Zn-finger domain linker. A phosphomimic mutant at Ser(322) decreased REST repressor activity and caused its transition to the cytosol, followed by degradation. Molecular dynamics simulations of the phosphomimic REST mutant revealed a sharp decrease in the stability of the REST-RE1 binding interface. Phosphorylation of REST by CaMKIV suppressed the downscaling of excitatory postsynaptic current (EPSC) frequency in response to hyperactivity. Moreover, the homeostatic effects of CaMKIV on EPSC amplitude were inhibited in the absence of REST. The results demonstrate that CaMKIV phosphorylation plays a crucial role in regulating REST levels and repressor activity and that an interplay exists between CaMKIV and REST in homeostatic plasticity mechanisms.

title: Disclosing pathogenic processes of monkeypox (MPOX) and drug repurposing through host-transcriptomics analysis.
authors: Mahmud, Sabkat; Ajadee, Alvira; Ali, Md Ahad; Ahmed, Md Feroj; Ahmmed, Reaz; Rana, Md Masud; Noor, Tasfia; Faysal, Md Fahim; Kabir, Md Hadiul; Mollah, Md Nurul Haque
abstract: Monkeypox (MPOX) virus infection outbreak in Africa in 2022 was initially considered a neglected tropical disease (NTD). Now it is recognized as a global health problem. The recent global spread has emphasized the need for increased attention to combat MPOX. Although there are some vaccines against MPOX, most people worldwide are still not vaccinated due to their unawareness or unavailability. However, so far, there is no approved drug against MPOX yet. Therefore, effective drugs against MPOX are also essential. This study attempted to disclose pathogenic processes and therapeutic strategies of MPOX based on MPOX-associated host key-genes (hKGs). At first, three transcriptomic profile datasets were analyzed, identifying 166 common host differentially expressed genes (hDEGs) between MPOX patients and control groups, comprising 75 upregulated and 91 downregulated hDEGs. Subsequently, six top-ranked host key genes (hKGs): ALB, HSP90AA1, CDH1, PTPRC, IGF1, and ABL1, were identified as potential MPOX-causing genes through protein-protein interaction (PPI) network analysis. Functional enrichment analysis of these hKGs revealed critical pathogenic processes of MPOX infection, including biological processes, molecular functions, cellular components, and KEGG pathways. Regulatory network analysis involving transcription factors and miRNAs provided further insights into disease mechanisms. Based on molecular docking analysis, five top-ranked drug molecules Tecovirimat, Beclabuvir, Maraviroc, Raltegravir, and Brincidofovir were identified as potential repurposable therapeutics against MPOX. ADME/T and drug-likeness evaluations confirmed favorable pharmacokinetic properties for these candidates. Additionally, 100 ns molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of the top three complexes (ALB-Tecovirimat, CDH1-Maraviroc, and PPARG-Beclabuvir) demonstrated strong binding stability, supported by RMSD, RMSF, and MM-GBSA results. Therefore, the results provided in this study might be potential resources for diagnosis and therapies of MPOX patients. However, the findings require experimental validation in wet lab for further confirmation.

title: Inferring gene regulatory networks from single-cell transcriptomics jointly through graph neural networks and Transformer.
authors: Gan, Yanglan; Liu, Tao; Xu, Guangwei; Guo, Wenjing; Zou, Guobing
journal: IEEE transactions on computational biology and bioinformatics
abstract: Inferring gene regulatory networks (GRNs) is crucial for understanding the complex regulatory relationships that govern gene expression in cells. Recently, several computational methods have been proposed for reconstructing GRNs from single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data. However, most of these methods primarily focus on pairwise regulatory relationships between genes, failing to leverage the global regulatory structure of GRNs, which is crucial for exploring the complex regulatory interactions between transcription factors (TFs) and their target genes. To address these limitations, we propose GTGRNS, a supervised learning framework that integrates a graph neural network with a Transformer encoder for GRN inference from scRNA-seq data. Specifically, we utilize the GraphSAGE model to integrate regulatory network topological information with gene expression features, facilitating the learning of gene representations. By leveraging the Transformer model, we further extract complex dependencies of gene pairs, which are crucial for determining regulatory levels. The comparative experiments on several benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and competitiveness of the proposed GTGRNS in the task of GRN inference.

title: From Genes to Diets: A Critical Review of Genetic, Nutrigenomic and Epigenetic Mechanisms in Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
authors: Araujo, Rafael G; Ortiz-Cruz, Gabriela; Nupo, Sunday Sedodo; Cordero, Yulianna; Cortes-Hernandez, Lauro; Teniente, Sandra Lucia
abstract: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2D) represents over 90% of diabetes cases globally, posing a growing public health crisis with an estimated 783 million adults projected to be affected by 2045. This condition arises from a complex interplay of insulin resistance, progressive pancreatic beta-cell dysfunction, and chronic low-grade inflammation, strongly influenced by genetic predisposition, obesity, sedentary lifestyle, and poor dietary habits. While genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified key susceptibility loci, including TCF7L2, PPARG, and KCNJ11, these varian0ts explain only ~10% of T2D heritability, underscoring the critical role of gene-environment interactions. This review synthesizes current evidence on the genetic, nutrigenomic, and epigenetic mechanisms underlying T2D pathogenesis and progression. We examine how dietary components, such as flavonoids, terpenoids, alkaloids, and bioactive compounds from natural products, modulate gene expression via transcription factors and influence insulin sensitivity, oxidative stress, and inflammation. Furthermore, we explore the emerging role of epigenetic modifications, including DNA methylation, histone acetylation, and chromatin remodeling, in mediating the lasting effects of hyperglycemia and environmental factors on T2D risk. The potential of epigenetic biomarkers for early diagnosis, patient stratification, and personalized therapy is discussed. Finally, we highlight how next-generation sequencing and artificial intelligence, particularly machine learning and deep learning models, are advancing multi-omics data integration, enabling improved T2D subtype classification, prognosis prediction, and the development of precision nutrition and pharmacoepigenetic strategies.

title: Integrated Transcriptomic and Network Analysis Identifies Candidate Kinase-Mediated Thyroid-Associated Targets of Withaferin A.
authors: Abdullah, Ejlal Mohamed; Alameen, Alaa Alnoor; AlAfaleq, Nouf Omar; Alharbi, Mona Shujaa
abstract: Withaferin A (WA), a bioactive steroidal lactone derived from Withania somnifera, has been reported to exhibit diverse pharmacological activities, including anti-inflammatory and metabolic regulatory effects. Although previous studies suggest a potential link between WA and thyroid-related molecular pathways, the molecular mechanisms underlying these effects remain incompletely understood. Here, we employed a comprehensive computational approach to explore WA-responsive molecular changes potentially relevant to thyroid-associated processes. RNA-sequencing data from WA-treated MCF-10A human mammary epithelial cells (GSE158085) were analysed to identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs). Because thyroid-specific WA transcriptomic datasets are not currently available, the DEGs were intersected with curated hypothyroidism-associated genes to generate a cross-tissue, exploratory set of candidate genes. The genes that overlapped were used to construct protein-protein interaction networks, prioritize high-centrality candidate genes, and conduct enrichment analyses for transcription factors and kinases. Further analysis of selected upstream kinases was performed using molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations with WA. A total of 1458 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified, 10 of which overlapped with hypothyroidism-associated genes. Network analysis identified candidate interactions among the overlapping genes, while higher-confidence analysis retained four connected genes (PTPN22, STAT4, DUOX2, and DUOXA2). Transcription factor enrichment identified ERG, SUZ12, NANOG, TCF3, RUNX1, and TP63 as potential upstream regulators, while kinase enrichment identified candidate upstream kinases associated with the predicted regulatory network. Based on enrichment evidence, structural availability, and literature-supported biological relevance, MAPK14 (p38alpha), AKT1, and MAPK8 (JNK1) were selected for molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations. Structural analyses suggested potential interactions between WA and the selected kinases, with target-specific dynamic behaviour across the simulated systems. Collectively, the findings highlight WA-responsive genes and predicted gene-TF-kinase relationships that may be relevant to thyroid-associated molecular processes. However, these associations are hypothesis-generating and provide a basis for further investigation in thyroid-derived experimental models.

title: Nanoscale Analysis of SSB-RecO Interplay in SSB Interaction with the Target.
authors: Irukuvajjula, Shivkumar Sharma; Filliaux, Shaun; Lyubchenko, Yuri L
abstract: Single-stranded DNA-binding protein (SSB) coats single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) and recruits downstream factors, yet this same coating must be cleared for SSB-interacting proteins to bind. RecA is a central protein in homologous recombination, which requires SSB-free ssDNA to load during the process. RecO, a recombination mediator protein, is thought to regulate this handoff, but it has not been shown directly that RecO drives the release of full-length, ssDNA-bound SSB. Using atomic force microscopy, we show that RecO actively displaces full-length wild-type SSB from a defined ssDNA substrate, reducing occupancy from 67% to 29%. Displacement efficiency decreases after deleting the C-terminal tip of SSB (DeltaC8) or after adding a single alanine at the C-terminus of SSB (A179). Molecular dynamics simulations show that A179 retains its native RecO contact but additionally engages a non-native surface, producing a specific, over-engaged complex, suggesting that these interprotein interactions may affect SSB-ssDNA contacts. Together, these findings suggest that RecO-driven SSB clearance is governed by the protein-protein interface rather than by ssDNA-binding affinity alone, thereby acting as a checkpoint against indiscriminate SSB removal during genome maintenance.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Plant Gene Regulatory Networks.
authors: Yu, Haopeng
abstract: Gene regulatory networks (GRNs) are the maps that plant biologists most want to draw, with arrows pointing from transcription factors to the genes they control, explaining how plants develop and respond to the environment. Since experimental validation of even one arrow can take years, and a single plant genome harbours tens of millions of candidate TF-target pairs, this gap has driven the development of numerous computational methods for GRN inference. Here I review three generations of computational approaches to plant GRN inference and measure them against a five-level ladder of evidence, including statistical association, conditional dependence, physical binding, functional regulation and causal circuits. Classical statistics and machine learning have simplified complex gene expression data into clear, prioritised predictions. Techniques like single-cell and multi-omics methods help uncover cell type-specific networks based on chromatin accessibility and binding motifs. Now, deep learning can interpret cis-regulatory grammar directly from genome sequences, and foundation models trained on plant genomes and millions of cells hold exciting potential to share regulatory insights across different species. The most promising route forward is a lab-in-the-loop division of labour in which foundation models serve not as oracles but as hypothesis engines, collapsing fifty million candidate TF-target pairs into the few hundred edges most worth the bench's time, with each round of validation sharpening the next round of prediction.

title: Spatiotemporal Multi-Omics and Compartment-Resolved Metabolomic Analyses Reveal the Mechanisms and Core Regulatory Networks of Cuticular Wax Formation in Blueberry Fruits.
authors: Chen, Shaopeng; Cheng, Yuxuan; Zhuang, Qianqian; Zhang, Yujie
abstract: The cuticular wax (bloom) of blueberries is crucial for postharvest storability and commercial value, yet the regulatory networks underlying its formation remain elusive. Here, we integrated scanning electron microscopy (SEM) with transcriptomic and compartment-resolved metabolomic analyses to elucidate the dynamic establishment of epicuticular wax in blueberry 'Bluecrop'. SEM revealed an ordered transition of wax crystals from a sparse fibrous structure at the green stage to a dense sponge-like three-dimensional network at maturity. Parallel untargeted liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) metabolomics of the whole fruit (intracellular precursor pool) and epicuticular wax (extracellular assembly layer) captured the spatiotemporal surge of key triterpenoids, such as oleanolic and ursolic acids, the major constituents associated with wax crystal coarsening. Through weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) and LASSO machine learning, we identified co-expression modules, most notably Turquoise, that were closely associated with lipid and triterpenoid synthesis. Hub genes, including a putative VcMYB96 transcription factor and plasma membrane-localized VcABCG-like transporters, are hypothesized to mediate carbon flux reallocation and transmembrane export of hydrophobic precursors. This study provides a "phenotype-transcriptome-metabolome" framework and candidate targets for functional validation and molecular breeding of blueberry cultivars with superior bloom traits.

title: Calycosin Attenuates LPS-Induced Cardiomyocyte Injury Through Regulation of the PPARgamma/NF-kappaB Signaling Pathway.
authors: Zhao, Rui; Wang, Zhiwang; Liu, Wuzhou; Liang, Keke
abstract: Calycosin (CAL) is an isoflavone monomer derived from Astragalus membranaceus that possesses potent anti-inflammatory and antioxidative pharmacological activities. However, the specific role of CAL in lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced inflammatory injury in cardiomyocytes remains to be elucidated. In this study, we established an in vitro inflammatory injury model using LPS-stimulated H9c2 cardiomyocytes to evaluate the cardioprotective effects of CAL. We assessed cell viability, live/dead cell staining, oxidative stress markers, inflammatory cytokine profiles, and cardiac injury biomarkers to characterize the protective efficacy of CAL. Quantitative proteomics combined with bioinformatics analysis was employed to explore the underlying mechanisms. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations were performed to analyze the predicted binding affinity and complex stability between CAL and the target proteins PPARgamma and NF-kappaB. PPARgamma and NF-kappaB mRNA and protein levels were measured by qPCR and Western blotting, and rescue experiments with the PPARgamma-specific inhibitor GW9662 were performed to validate target dependency. Our results demonstrated that CAL exerted significant protective effects against LPS-induced cardiomyocyte injury, effectively enhancing cell viability, reducing cell death, alleviating intracellular ROS accumulation, modulating oxidative stress-related parameters, suppressing excessive inflammatory responses, and decreasing the release of cardiac injury biomarkers. Proteomic analysis revealed that differentially expressed proteins were significantly enriched in the PPAR signaling pathway. Molecular simulations predicted that CAL binds stably to both PPARgamma and NF-kappaB. PCR and Western blotting results showed that CAL upregulated PPARgamma and suppressed NF-kappaB-mediated pro-inflammatory gene expression at both the mRNA and protein levels. Notably, pharmacological blockade of PPARgamma with GW9662 partially abolished the cardioprotective effects of CAL. Collectively, these findings indicate that CAL ameliorates LPS-induced inflammatory injury in H9c2 cardiomyocytes through a protective mechanism that depends on activation of PPARgamma and subsequent inhibition of the NF-kappaB signaling pathway.

title: Identification of Imidazole-Benzenesulfonamide Derivatives with Anti-Inflammatory Activity Through Modulation of NF-kappaB Signaling.
authors: Kavaliauskas, Povilas; Vainauskas, Valdas; Petraitis, Vidmantas; Petraitiene, Ruta; Acevedo, Waldo; Grigaleviciute, Ramune; Grybaite, Birute; Golciene, Bozena; Stankevicius, Rolandas; Rakickas, Julius; Mickevicius, Vytautas
abstract: Inflammatory disorders remain an important therapeutic challenge, highlighting the need to identify novel small molecules capable of modulating inflammatory signaling. In this study, an in-house library of aromatic and heterocyclic drug-like compounds was screened for inhibition of lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced nuclear factor kappa B (NF-kappaB) activation using THP-1 dual-reporter cells. Eight compounds markedly suppressed NF-kappaB activity, and five structurally related 4-phenylimidazole-based benzenesulfonamide derivatives (1232, 1239, 1241, 1242, and 1245) were prioritized based on their cytotoxicity profiles. Functional activity was subsequently evaluated in LPS-stimulated RAW 264.7 macrophages. The selected compounds reduced nitrite production, attenuated LPS-induced nuclear localization of NF-kappaB, and differentially affected IL-6, KC/CXCL1, and TNF-alpha production. The naphthyl-substituted derivative 1239 showed prominent inhibition of nitrite, IL-6, and KC/CXCL1 production, whereas the ethylthio derivative 1232 preferentially reduced TNF-alpha. Molecular docking against a panel of inflammation-associated proteins revealed favorable predicted interactions of compound 1239 with IkappaB kinase(IKK) and p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase (p38 MAPK), with docking scores of -10.3 kcal/mol for both proteins and binding poses overlapping the corresponding crystallographic ligand-binding regions. Collectively, these findings identify 4-phenylimidazole-based benzenesulfonamides as a promising chemical series with anti-inflammatory activity and suggest IKK and p38 MAPK as potential components of the affected signaling network. Further structure-activity and mechanistic studies are required to define the molecular targets and optimize the activity of this compound class.

title: Green Extraction and Molecular Docking-Guided Discovery of Asiaticoside as a Multi-Target Modulator of the SIRT1/HMGB1/p53-p21 Axis in H(2)O(2)-Induced Senescent Endothelial Cells.
authors: Li, Wenkai; Huang, Jianhua; Zeng, Fei; Wang, Yuping; Liu, Xiong; Wang, Junjie; Liu, Siyu
abstract: Endothelial cell senescence is a key contributor to vascular ageing and cardiovascular diseases. Asiaticoside, a pentacyclic triterpenoid saponin from Centella asiatica, exhibits anti-inflammatory and antioxidant activities, yet its potential to modulate endothelial senescence remains unexplored. Herein, we report the molecular docking-guided discovery of asiaticoside as a multi-target modulator of the SIRT1/HMGB1/p53-p21 senescence regulatory axis. Asiaticoside was isolated via a green acid-hydrolysis strategy using dilute HCl as the extraction solvent, followed by polyamide enrichment and C(18) reversed-phase purification (purity > 98%). Molecular docking revealed that asiaticoside binds favourably to SIRT1 (-8.1 kcal mol(-1)), the HMGB1-DNA complex (-10.7 kcal mol(-1)), and several senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP)-related inflammatory cytokines. In H(2)O(2)-induced senescent human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs), asiaticoside at 100 muM significantly reduced senescence-associated beta-galactosidase activity and alleviated G0/G1 cell cycle arrest without cytotoxicity. Mechanistically, asiaticoside restored SIRT1 expression, suppressed the secretion of IL-1beta, IL-6, IL-8, TNF-alpha, and HMGB1, downregulated p21 at both mRNA and protein levels, reduced p53 protein expression, and suppressed p16 mRNA expression. These findings demonstrate that asiaticoside attenuates endothelial senescence and SASP-driven inflammation, an effect associated with restoration of SIRT1 expression and suppression of the HMGB1/p53-p21 pathway.

title: Design, Synthesis and Antitumor Activity Evaluation of Novel Dual G9a/EZH2 Inhibitors.
authors: Shi, Yajie; Zhang, Qiuyue; Zhang, Maoying; Zhao, Xiujuan; Zhang, Shuhang; Li, Jirui; Li, Haofeng; Fu, Chenglin; Chen, Guoliang
abstract: Targeting the crosstalk between histone methyltransferases G9a and EZH2 represents a promising strategy for cancer therapy. To improve upon our previously reported dual inhibitor SU08, we rationally designed and synthesized five series (SU, UA, UB, N, and L) of novel G9a/EZH2 dual inhibitors, incorporating diverse pyridone, urea, and thienopyrimidine moieties, yielding a total of 43 compounds. In vitro enzymatic screening revealed that compound SU101 against both EZH2 (IC(50) = 4.08 nM) and G9a (IC(50) = 2.92 nM) was comparable to SU08. Western blot analysis confirmed that SU101 and SU103 effectively suppressed both H3K27me3 and H3K9me2 expression in rhabdomyosarcoma RD cells. In cellular antiproliferative assays, SU101 showed the strongest activity (IC(50) = 15.33 muM). Molecular docking and dynamics simulations verified stable binding interactions between SU101 and both target proteins. Pharmacokinetic studies in rats demonstrated that SU101 possesses excellent oral bioavailability (94.3%), moderate plasma protein binding (84.6%), and an acceptable acute toxicity profile (LD(50) = 31.02 mg/kg in mice). Overall, these results suggest that SU101 may serve as a promising lead compound for further optimization and support the continued exploration of dual G9a/EZH2 inhibitors as a potential therapeutic approach for rhabdomyosarcoma.

title: Deep Learning and Domain Expertise for Fabricating High-Performance Biosensors.
authors: Xiao, Mei-Ling; Zhang, Pengcheng; Li, Zhijie; Lin, Nuo-Qiao; Wang, Xiaowo; Liu, Jian-Zhong
abstract: Transcription factor-based biosensors are essential for the scalable bioproduction of plant natural products. However, a major bottleneck in developing high-performance biosensors is the engineering of responsive promoters due to the vast sequence space and poorly understood sequence-function relationships. Here, we extend our previously published DeepSEED framework into an artificial intelligence-driven pipeline for efficient and extensible biosensor-responsive promoter optimization. This strategy integrates deep learning with domain-specific biological expertise. By fixing core promoter elements, varying the number and position of transcription factor binding sites (TFBSs) to define promoter backbones, and subsequently optimizing the flanking sequences, we enable the de novo design of promoters. We systematically apply this strategy to optimize a panel of biosensors across different transcription factors and regulatory modes, including four metabolite-responsive biosensors and a quorum-sensing-based environmental sensor. The resulting biosensors exhibit diverse dynamic behaviors with markedly improved sensitivity, expanded dynamic range, and increased maximum output. For instance, the optimized naringenin biosensor demonstrates a 32-fold broader dynamic range and a 27-fold higher maximum output compared to its parent. To illustrate its utility in metabolic engineering, we employed a DeepSEED-designed promoter to dynamically regulate a p-coumaric acid biosynthesis pathway, boosting production by 117.0%. Our work extends the previously published DeepSEED framework into a powerful pipeline for biosensor optimization and delivers a portfolio of high-performance regulatory elements, addressing a critical need and facilitating the development of more intelligent and productive metabolic engineering systems.

title: Integration by parts: The multi-layered mechanisms of cis-regulatory control.
authors: Cornwall-Scoones, Jake; Briscoe, James; Delas, M Joaquina
abstract: Cis-regulatory elements (CREs) integrate signals from transcription factors (TFs) to control gene expression, yet mechanisms underlying this information processing remain poorly understood. Deep learning demonstrates expression is predictable from CRE sequence, suggesting that unifying principles of regulation are within reach. Here, we propose a framework dividing CRE regulatory logic into two layers: binding-level integration, where cooperative TF interactions modulate DNA occupancy; and transcriptional-level integration, where TF effector domains and cofactors convert binding configurations into expression. At the binding level, we classify TF cooperativity along orthogonal axes-specific versus general, and symmetric versus asymmetric-encompassing protein-protein interactions, nucleosome competition, pioneer activity, and assisted loading. At the transcriptional level, cofactor interactions generate additive, synergistic, or antagonistic logic. Emerging from this complexity is a recurring quantitative pattern: "multiplication plus saturation," reconciling binding specificity with flexibility, explaining how short DNA motifs generate precise expression while maintaining evolvability, and informing synthetic biology and therapeutic applications.

title: Integrative multi-omics analysis reveals the PFAS-gut microbiome-FN1 axis in chronic kidney disease: From exposome to therapeutic target.
authors: Li, Dandan; Yin, Jingya; Zhou, Hui; Ge, Nan; Wang, Bingling; Wang, Tianyi
abstract: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are persistent environmental pollutants associated with chronic kidney disease (CKD), yet the molecular mechanisms linking PFAS exposure to renal fibrosis remain incompletely understood. We developed a Chemical-Microbiome-Metabolite-Target-Pathway-Disease (C-M-M-T-P-D) network framework integrating differential expression analysis of real GEO transcriptomic data (GSE104954, n = 195 kidney biopsies), gene set enrichment analysis across four pathway databases, two-sample Mendelian randomization with four complementary methods, molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulation of deoxycholic acid (DCA) to fibronectin 1 (FN1), and transcription factor and protein-protein interaction network analyses. FN1 was significantly upregulated in CKD (log(2)FC = 0.322, FDR = 6.67e-11), accompanied by elevated COL1A2, VIM, and POSTN, whereas TGFBR3 was downregulated (log(2)FC = -0.746, FDR = 1.67e-14). GSEA identified ECM-receptor interaction (NES = 2.23), interferon gamma response (NES = 2.70), and epithelial-mesenchymal transition (NES = 1.99) as top enriched pathways. MR analysis using real MiBioGen and CKDGen GWAS data (19 SNPs for Akkermansia, 12 SNPs for Desulfovibrio) revealed contrasting findings: Akkermansia to CKD showed no significant genetic association (0/4 methods, all p > 0.30), whereas Desulfovibrio to CKD demonstrated a robust positive genetic association across all four methods (IVW p = 0.008, WM p = 4.70e-04, MR-RAPS p = 1.46e-05, MR-cML p = 2.08e-06), though the significant Egger intercept (p = 0.005) for Desulfovibrio warrants cautious interpretation regarding pleiotropy. Molecular docking and 15-ns MD simulation confirmed stable DCA binding to FN1 (PDB: 2CG7, 1.20 A X-ray; MM/GBSA DeltaG(bind) = -32.4 kcal/mol). The C-M-M-T-P-D network positioned FN1 as the third highest-degree node, bridging metabolite and pathway layers. This integrative multi-omics analysis provides multi-omics evidence supporting the PFAS-gut microbiome-FN1 axis as a hypothesis-generating framework for understanding CKD pathogenesis, supported by transcriptomic, structural, and network-level evidence, with genetic associations warranting further experimental validation.

title: Structure-guided discovery of a dual JAK2/RAGE modulator reveals a computationally driven strategy for targeting convergent oncogenic signaling in renal cell carcinoma.
authors: Mohammad-Al-Shahrani, Mesfer; Abohassan, Mohammad; Rajagopalan, Prasanna
abstract: Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is driven by convergent inflammatory and proliferative signaling pathways. RAGE-mediated NF-kappaB activation and JAK2-STAT3 signaling cooperate to amplify cytokine production and oncogenic progression. Targeting these interconnected pathways represents a rational therapeutic strategy. High-throughput virtual screening of ChemBridge libraries, 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations, and MM/PBSA analysis were performed. The lead compound RJS6641 was evaluated using biochemical assays (HTRF JAK2 kinase assay, differential scanning fluorimetry), a cell-free AGE-RAGE binding ELISA, and functional assays in RCC cell lines, including viability, reporter, cytokine, apoptosis, and migration analyses. RJS6641 showed stable binding to JAK2 (protein RMSD  approximately 0.28 nm; ligand RMSD 0.15-0.20 nm) and RAGE (protein RMSD 0.50-1.50 nm; ligand RMSD 0.30-0.35 nm). It inhibited JAK2 in an ATP-competitive manner (IC(5)(0) = 60.23 nM; ruxolitinib IC(5)(0) = 1.69 nM), with ATP-dependent shifts (35.04 --> 74.09 --> 305.6 nM) and thermal stabilization (DeltaTm +1.50  degrees C). AGE-RAGE binding was disrupted (IC(5)(0) = 118.2 nM). RJS6641 reduced RCC viability (GI(5)(0): 799.8-2021 nM) while sparing HK-2 cells (GI(5)(0) 12,816 nM; 6-16x difference). It suppressed STAT3 (IC(5)(0) 412.3-813.2 nM) and NF-kappaB (IC(5)(0) 435.7-1031 nM) signaling, reduced IL-6/IL-8 secretion, induced caspase-3/7 activation (EC(5)(0) 662.4-862.9 nM), and inhibited migration (up to 83%). Collectively, RJS6641 functions as a JAK2 inhibitor with additional modulation of RAGE-associated signaling, leading to coordinated suppression of STAT3/NF-kappaB pathways and anti-tumor effects in RCC, supporting further in vivo and selectivity evaluation.

title: Network pharmacology-based investigation on the mechanism of aloin in ameliorating atherosclerosis by regulating macrophage polarization.
authors: Tian, Ye; Mei, Xianghui; Zeng, Fang; Li, Baichao; Du, Wentao; Chen, Xianru
abstract: Atherosclerosis (AS) is a chronic inflammatory vascular disease in which macrophage polarization plays a pivotal role in plaque progression and stability. Aloin, a major anthraquinone compound isolated from Aloe vera, possesses potent anti-inflammatory activities; however, its therapeutic potential and underlying mechanisms in AS remain insufficiently understood. In the present study, a network pharmacology approach combined with molecular docking, cellular experiments, and animal validation was employed to investigate the protective effects of aloin against AS and elucidate its molecular mechanism. Common targets shared by aloin, macrophage polarization, and AS were identified, followed by protein-protein interaction network construction and GO/KEGG enrichment analyses. Molecular docking demonstrated strong binding affinities of aloin toward key inflammatory targets, particularly NF-kappaB and STAT3. Experimental validation showed that aloin significantly suppressed nitric oxide production in lipopolysaccharide-induced RAW264.7 macrophages and inhibited M1 macrophage polarization while promoting the M2 phenotype, as evidenced by decreased expression of iNOS and TNF-alpha and increased expression of Arg-1 and IL-10. In ApoE-/- mice fed a high-fat diet, aloin markedly reduced aortic plaque formation and alleviated vascular pathological injury. Mechanistically, both in vitro and in vivo analyses revealed that aloin significantly attenuated the phosphorylation of NF-kappaB and STAT3, thereby blocking activation of the NF-kappaB/STAT3 signaling pathway. Collectively, these findings suggest that aloin may contribute to the amelioration of atherosclerotic lesions by modulating macrophage polarization balance through inhibition of NF-kappaB/STAT3 signaling, highlighting its potential as a candidate worthy of further investigation for the prevention and treatment of atherosclerosis.

title: Identification of Mitochondrial Dynamics-Related Genes as Diagnostic Biomarkers for Osteoarthritis Using Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis and Machine Learning.
authors: Wang, Hui; Zhang, Peng; Ren, Xinqiang; Tan, Kaitao; Qiu, Yongfeng; Li, Linqing
abstract: BACKGROUND: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a chronic, painful joint disease whose early diagnosis is critical for effective treatment. Since mitochondrial dynamics have been implicated in the onset and progression of OA, this study aimed to explore the diagnostic value of mitochondrial dynamics-related genes (MDRGs) in OA. METHODS: Weighted gene co-expression network analysis and 3 machine learning algorithms, including least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regression, support vector machine-recursive feature elimination, and Boruta, were used to screen signature genes. The intersection of genes identified by all 3 algorithms was taken as the candidate set. Expression levels of these genes were compared between OA and normal tissues, and receiver operating characteristic curves were used to validate their diagnostic performance, yielding final hub genes. An in vitro OA model was established, and the expression of key genes was validated using quantitative reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) and Western blot analysis. Immune infiltration in OA was assessed, and hub genes' functional analogs, microRNAs (miRNAs), transcription factors (TFs), and potential drugs were predicted. RESULTS: Two hub genes, CDH11 and MSX2, were identified. Both genes were up-regulated in OA and demonstrated promising diagnostic efficacy. qRT-PCR and Western blot validation revealed that mRNA and protein levels of CDH11 and MSX2 were significantly higher in OA cell models than in normal cells. Based on transcriptomic data, the single-sample gene set enrichment analysis algorithm inferred that significantly higher levels of B cells, macrophages, mast cells, neutrophils, T helper cells, and tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes were found in OA samples than in controls. Twenty functional analogs of the 2 hub genes were predicted, mainly enriched in skeletal system development and bone development functional pathways. Additionally, 34 miRNAs (e.g., hsa-miR-568, hsa-miR-548d-5p, hsa-miR-144) and 17 TFs (e.g., CEBPA, NFATC1, SP1, EGR1, FOXO1) were predicted based on CDH11 and MSX2. Entinostat, estradiol, cobaltous chloride, and valproic acid were identified as potential OA therapeutics. CONCLUSIONS: CDH11 and MSX2 may serve as candidate diagnostic biomarkers for OA, identified from a predefined MDRG set, but requiring further mechanistic and clinical validation.

title: Integrated multi-omics and genome mining strategies for activating cryptic polyketide biosynthetic gene clusters in Streptomyces: an overview.
authors: Santhoshkumar, R; Mohamed, Hafid; Jemo, Martin
abstract: Beneficial microbes from soil or marine habitats are promising sources for discovery of new bioactive compounds for medicine and agriculture, largely through biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) that encode the production of complex natural products for drug and antibiotic discovery. However, most BGCs are transcriptionally silent under standard testing conditions and may require a complex, integrated approach for activation. In this review, we revisit previous approaches to activating BGCs, focusing on polyketides. We additionally discuss how integrating genome mining strategies with multi-omics integration, synthetic biology methods, and precise genome-editing tools is providing increasingly precise strategies for the discovery and engineering of polyketide-producing Streptomyces. We further discuss how to couple artificial intelligence (AI)-designed promoters could enable the production of novel compounds with improved yields, expanded chemical diversity, and enhanced industrial potential. We further examine how state-of-the-art CRISPR-Cas systems, including base editing, facilitate precise editing of high-GC-content genomes while circumventing the genome instability and Cas9-associated cellular toxicity that frequently accompany double-strand break formation in Streptomyces, and how chromatin topology rewiring dismantles transcriptional silencing. Unlike reviews that address genome mining, pathway engineering, or genome editing as separate approaches, this review presents an integrated framework linking computational BGC prediction, multi-omics validation, and precision engineering to prioritize and activate cryptic polyketide pathways in Streptomyces. We propose comprehensive computational genomics prediction approaches and integrate them with experimental validation through promoter engineering, transcription factor decoys, and chassis strain optimization, highlighting how these methods and tools are advancing the field from descriptive BGC catalogs to scalable, predictive models for next-generation drug discovery. Future efforts to couple AI-generated, sequence-orthogonal promoter libraries with biology-based modeling hold great promise.

title: Hemin suppresses interferon responses in periodontal cell models through JAK2-STAT1 inhibition.
authors: Huang, Xiaoyu; Gruber, Reinhard; Panahipour, Layla
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Hemin, an oxidized heme species released during erythrocyte breakdown, is detectable in gingival crevicular fluid during periodontal inflammation, but its effects on local immune signaling remain unclear. We investigated whether hemin modifies cytokine-induced interferon responses in HSC-2 oral squamous cell carcinoma cells and primary human gingival fibroblasts. METHODS: Cells were stimulated with interleukin-1beta and tumor necrosis factor-alpha, or with interferon-gamma, in the presence or absence of hemin. Transcriptomic changes were assessed by RNA sequencing and pathway analysis, and selected transcripts and proteins were validated by reverse-transcription quantitative PCR, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, immunoblotting, and immunofluorescence. Ligand-kinase interactions were examined by molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations, and recombinant Janus kinase 2 activity was measured in a cell-free assay. RESULTS: Hemin preferentially suppressed an interferon-associated gene network, including CXCL10, CXCL11, MX1, OAS1, IFIT1, IFIT3, and ISG15, while nuclear factor kappaB-associated responses were comparatively preserved. Hemin also reduced signal transducer and activator of transcription 1 Tyr701 phosphorylation and nuclear accumulation induced by either the cytokine combination or interferon-gamma. Computational analyses predicted stable hemin interactions within conserved ATP-binding pockets of Janus kinases, and the cell-free assay demonstrated inhibition of recombinant Janus kinase 2. DISCUSSION: Together, these findings show that hemin attenuates interferon-associated transcription in periodontal cell models, consistent with inhibition of the Janus kinase 2-signal transducer and activator of transcription 1 axis. This mechanism may enable blood-derived hemin to modify local mucosal immune signaling, although its relevance to periodontal tissues and antiviral defense requires confirmation in organotypic, infection, and in vivo models.

title: A Hybrid Machine Learning Ensemble for Predicting Genetic Predisposition to Lung Cancer Based on Polymorphisms in the Mismatch DNA Repair Genes.
authors: Bagla, Abhay; Singh, Sidhartha; Kansal, Heena; Gupta, Anup Kumar; Sharma, Siddharth; Gupta, Puneet; Gupta, Vivek
abstract: The application of machine learning approaches has shown promising results in cancer prediction. In the present study, data for nine gene-based features that include MLH1 (rs1800734), MSH3 (rs26279), MSH6 (rs3136228), and several variants within MSH2 (rs2303423, rs4987188, rs17217772, rs63749993, rs2303426, and rs2303428), along with four additional features (Age, Gender, Smoking, and Pack Years) were used as input to develop a predictive model for assessing individual susceptibility to lung cancer. NumPy, Pandas, Scikit-learn, and Matplotlib were major libraries used during the modeling process. The models included CatBoost, XGBoost, gradient boosting, random forest, support vector machine (SVM), K-nearest neighbors (KNN), Gaussian Naive Bayes, and logistic regression, with their performance evaluated using stratified 5-fold cross-validation. The highest accuracy in predicting cancer predisposition was achieved by CatBoost (0.831 +/- 0.014), with Pack Years (27.94%), Age (10.75%), and MLH1 (9.97%) as the major predictors. Precision, recall, and F1-score were also used to assess performance, and all were within the range of 0.83-0.84. The models were further tested for performance across histological subtypes, gender, and smoking status. Gradient Boosting (0.868 +/- 0.028) and Random Forest (0.902 +/- 0.020) yielded the highest accuracy as histological subtype classifiers in ADCC and SCLC, respectively. When modeled using sex-stratified and smoking-status-specific models, the ensemble methods significantly outperformed logistic regression and Gaussian Naive Bayes, with MMR gene variants (MLH1, MSH2) emerging as key modulators of histology and risk stratification. This highlights the potential of ensemble methods to bridge the gap between genetic epidemiology and molecular pathology, enabling more accurate risk assessment.

title: Investigating potential prognostic genes and candidate therapeutic targets for acute myeloid leukemia in food-medicine homologous plants via integrated network pharmacology and transcriptomics.
authors: Tang, Mingxia; Chen, Tao; Huang, Tao; Bai, Shanshan; Wang, Yajiang; Zhang, Yanling; Yan, Lian; He, Xia
abstract: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a hematologic malignancy. Conventional chemotherapy often causes substantial adverse effects, while food-medicine homologous plants with favorable safety profiles and multitarget regulatory activities offer a promising strategy for AML treatment. This study aimed to screen core bioactive compounds from 106 food-medicine homologous plants, identify potential prognostic genes related to AML, and explore the molecular mechanisms of their anti-AML activities. Public omics cohorts for AML were systematically analyzed to screen differentially expressed genes (DEGs). The DEGs were intersected with the target genes of 106 food-medicine homologous plants to obtain candidate genes for subsequent GO/KEGG functional enrichment analysis and PPI network analysis. Core bioactive compounds were screened and prioritized via the Graph-based Bilinear Attention Network (GraphBAN) combined with druggability and toxicology screening criteria. Potential prognostic genes were identified via univariate Cox proportional hazards regression analysis and further screening. Immune infiltration analysis and gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) were performed on the identified potential prognostic genes. Bioinformatic prediction was conducted to identify upstream transcription factors (TFs) and microRNAs (miRNAs) targeting these genes and to analyze their chromosomal distribution and subcellular localization characteristics. Binding affinity and stability between core active compounds and proteins encoded by potential prognostic genes were systematically confirmed by molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulation analyses. The expression levels of potential prognostic genes were finally validated via reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR). We identified 1102 candidate genes, 542 core bioactive compounds, and 6 potential prognostic genes. The constructed prognostic model demonstrated moderate predictive performance. Immune infiltration analysis identified 18 types of differentially infiltrated immune-cell populations (P < 0.05), and GSEA results indicated that immunity-related signaling pathways were enriched in the AML high-risk subgroup. Moreover, 138 chemotherapeutic agents were identified. MYB-centered transcription factors and numerous microRNAs were found to regulate these potential prognostic genes. The genes reside on distinct chromosomes; for example, ITGB3 is located on chromosome 17. Further subcellular localization analysis revealed distinct protein distribution patterns. IGF1R, ITGB3, and SLC38A1 are predominantly located on the cell membrane, while KYNU, PDE4A, and GSTM2 are mostly located in the cytoplasm. Molecular docking revealed that the binding energy between IGF1R and MOL008397 was - 10.7 kcal/mol. Molecular dynamics simulation further confirmed the stability of this molecular complex. RT-qPCR verified distinct expression of the six prognostic genes in clinical AML blood samples. This study identified core active compounds and potential prognostic genes against AML derived from food-medicine homologous plants, which provides evidence for prognosis evaluation and targeted therapy.

title: Deep learning uncovers hidden power of low-affinity motifs.
authors: Bower, Grace; Kvon, Evgeny Z
abstract: Low-affinity transcription factor binding sites are functionally important but difficult to map and mechanistically poorly understood. In this issue of Cell Genomics, Weilert et al. leverage sequence-to-function deep learning models to systematically map low-affinity pioneer factor binding sites in mouse embryonic stem cells and reveal how these sites contribute to chromatin opening through soft-syntax nucleosomal cooperativity.

title: QingGanJianPi oral solution ameliorates hyperlipidemia by facilitating crosstalk between multiple active metabolites and the PPARalpha-LXRalpha axis.
authors: Wang, Jinji; Jing, Chenxu; Han, Yuna; Zhu, Zhijie; Yang, Ming; Zhuang, Xuefeng; Zhou, Kaixuan; Liu, Jia; Li, Lijing
journal: The Journal of pharmacy and pharmacology
abstract: OBJECTIVES: QingGanJianPi oral solution (QGJP), a traditional Chinese patent medicine, exhibits lipid-lowering and hepatoprotective effects. This study aimed to elucidate the mechanisms by which QGJP promotes lipid and cholesterol efflux. METHODS: Drug efficacy was evaluated in HFD-mice. Serum metabolomics combined with network pharmacology was performed to predict the relative signaling pathways involved. Molecular docking and thermal stability assays were conducted to identify active ingredients interacting with potential targets. The mRNA levels and protein expression were analyzed by qPCR and Western blotting. KEY FINDING: QGJP significantly reduced serum lipid levels in a dose-dependent manner. It also effectively attenuated high-fat diet-induced body weight gain and fat deposition. Untargeted serum metabolomics combined with network pharmacology revealed activation of the PPARalpha-LXRalpha-ABCA1 signaling axis following treatment. Among the circulating metabolites, salvianolic acid A was found to activate PPARalpha, thereby promoting the interaction between PPARalpha and LXRalpha, and enhancing the expression of downstream target genes. Furthermore, emodin upregulates ABCA1 expression mainly through direct activation of LXRalpha, with limited dependence on PPARalpha. CONCLUSIONS: Salvianolic acid A and emodin upregulate ABCA1 expression via multiple mechanisms, including direct activation of LXRalpha or activation through PPARalpha, thereby demonstrating the multi-target advantages of traditional Chinese medicine and providing preliminary insights into the synergistic interactions among its complex metabolites.

title: Fingolimod Alleviates Neuroinflammation and Blood-Brain Barrier Disruption in Epilepsy by Upregulating S1PR5 and Inhibiting the Rho/ROCK/NF-kappaB Pathway.
authors: Zhang, Chen; Duan, Yanli; Ma, Mengmeng; Xu, Lin; Jin, Wei-Na; Zhang, Zhuoran
abstract: OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to clarify the role of sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor 5 (S1PR5) in epileptic pathogenesis and the mechanism by which fingolimod exerts anti-epileptic effects, with a focus on neuroinflammation and blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption. METHODS: Multi-omics integration and machine learning were used to identify S1PR5 as a key candidate gene. Molecular docking was performed to verify the binding affinity between fingolimod and S1PR5. AAV-mediated S1PR5 overexpression was conducted in mouse hippocampi before kainic acid (KA) administration. KA-induced epileptic mice were randomly divided into control, model, and fingolimod intervention groups. Behavioral tests, qRT-PCR, Western blot, immunofluorescence, ELISA, and Evans Blue assay were used for evaluations. RESULTS: S1PR5 expression was significantly downregulated in both epileptic patients and mouse hippocampi. Fingolimod bound stably to S1PR5 in silico. S1PR5 overexpression attenuated neuronal loss, microglial activation, and epileptic seizures in KA-treated mice, confirming that S1PR5 exerts protective effects in epilepsy. Fingolimod intervention upregulated S1PR5 expression, inhibited abnormal activation of the Rho/ROCK/NF-kappaB pathway, restored tight junction proteins (Claudin-5 and ZO-1), reduced BBB leakage, and lowered proinflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, IL-6). These changes were accompanied by alleviated seizure severity and frequency. CONCLUSION: S1PR5 serves as a protective regulator in epilepsy. Fingolimod exerts anti-epileptic effects by upregulating S1PR5, thereby inhibiting the Rho/ROCK/NF-kappaB pathway, reducing neuroinflammation, and preserving BBB integrity. These findings support S1PR5 as a promising target and provide a mechanistic basis for repurposing fingolimod in epilepsy therapy.

title: In silico and Network Pharmacology Identification of Acacia senegal Phytochemicals as Potential alpha-Amylase Inhibitors.
authors: Abdu, Abdulkadir; Bakrey, Hossamaldeen; Rikabi, Hind A; Ali, Amani Ahmed Osman; Abdelrahim, Israa; Abdulkareem, Eman M; Eltaib, Lina
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Diabetes mellitus is a rapidly expanding chronic disease, prompting interest in plant-derived natural products as adjuncts to conventional therapy because of their improvements in glycaemic control and reduced complications. To evaluate phytochemicals' potential as alpha-amylase inhibitors using an integrated in-silico workflow. METHODS: Acacia senegal phytochemicals retrieved from the IMPPAT 2.0 database were evaluated their in-silico studies against alpha-amylase inhibitors using molecular docking, DFT, pharmacokinetic and toxicity profiling, in addition to PASS prediction, network pharmacology and MD simulations. RESULTS: Docking of 31 compounds was carried out, and the top three ligands, which are: IMPHY014840 (-9.321 kcal/mol), IMPHY014838 (-9.208 kcal/mol) and IMPHY006972 (-9.026 kcal/mol), were selected. Their favorable binding energies indicated strong predicted affinity toward the selected enzyme target. DFT calculations showed identical HOMO-LUMO gaps of 6.936 eV for the first two ligands, whereas the third one displayed a larger gap of 9.484 eV, indicating lower chemical reactivity. Furthermore, pharmacokinetic screening indicated high human intestinal absorption (75-86 %) and favorable Caco-2 permeability for the top three compounds, particularly for IMPHY014840 and IMPHY014838. PASS analysis suggested protease target affinity for IMPHY014840 and GPCR/transcription factor activity for IMPHY014838, expanding their therapeutic scope beyond alpha-amylase inhibition. MD trajectories confirmed overall complex stability, with IMPHY014838 exhibiting marginally lower ligand RMSD and therefore slightly superior dynamical stability. DISCUSSION: The present study identified IMPHY014840 and IMPHY014838 as promising alpha- amylase inhibitors, with docking scores of -9.321 and -9.208 kcal/mol, respectively. DFT, ADMET, toxicity, PASS, and 100 ns MD simulations indicate stable enzyme-ligand binding, high predicted intestinal absorption, and multitarget potential. Network pharmacology further suggests that these compounds act on a broad set of diabetes related targets, supporting their value as antidiabetic lead candidates. CONCLUSION: The combined computational evidence supports IMPHY014840 and IMPHY014838 as promising natural alpha-amylase inhibitors for type 2 DM management, and recommends in vitro, in vivo, and formulation optimization to address their limitations.

title: Machine Learning-Guided Identification of Madecassoside as a Potential RAD51 Modulator That Sensitizes Breast Cancer Cells to Cisplatin.
authors: Oh, Minju; Jeong, Mi-Young; Choi, Jiwon
abstract: Homologous recombination (HR) is an essential pathway for preserving the genomic stability of cells by repairing DNA damage, especially double-strand breaks and interstrand crosslinks. RAD51 recombinase plays a central role in the HR pathway, and when DNA damage occurs, RAD51 binds to single-stranded DNA at the cleavage site to form a helical nucleoprotein filament. Therefore, pharmacological inhibition of RAD51 is emerging as an attractive strategy to block the repair mechanisms of cancer cells and maximize the therapeutic efficacy of conventional radiation and chemotherapy. Several RAD51 small-molecule inhibitors, including CYT-0851, B02, and IBR2, have demonstrated preclinical or early clinical efficacy, but no candidate has yet received regulatory approval. In this study, we identified a novel RAD51 inhibitor from a natural product library using an in silico workflow that combines machine learning models and molecular docking simulations. Among the five machine learning models evaluated, the random forest (RF) model showed the best overall predictive performance after SMOTE-based class balancing and near-zero variance filtering, achieving an accuracy of 0.933, sensitivity of 0.800, specificity of 1.000, Cohen's kappa of 0.842, and ROC-AUC of 0.980. Using an optimized RF model, 1142 natural compounds were virtually screened, and Madecassoside was finally selected by molecular docking analysis. Biological validation showed that MDA-MB-231 cells increased susceptibility to cisplatin after Madecassoside treatment and also markedly inhibited the formation of RAD51 foci induced by cisplatin, strongly inhibiting DNA damage repair. These findings suggest that Madecassoside is a promising RAD51-modulating lead compound that may enhance cisplatin sensitivity by impairing RAD51-mediated DNA repair.

title: PF4 drives mechanical overload-induced temporomandibular joint osteoarthritis through TLR2-dependent activation of NF-kappaB.
authors: Sun, Wei; Wu, Jiashun; Liu, Yu; Li, Xiang; Zeng, Guozhong; Li, Kan; Su, Kai; Xia, Juan; Zheng, Guangsen
abstract: BACKGROUND: Mechanical overload‑related cytokines contribute to temporomandibular joint osteoarthritis (TMJOA) pathogenesis. This study investigated the role of overload‑associated platelet factor 4 (PF4). METHODS: Combined proteomic screening of human TMJOA synovial fluid (SF) and finite element simulation identified mechanically linked cytokines. A rat unilateral anterior crossbite (UAC) model was used to induce TMJ cartilage degeneration. To dissect the mechanism, primary rat TMJ chondrocytes were treated with PF4 and analyzed by transcriptomics and functional assays. Further, specific inhibitors targeting the canonical nuclear factor‑kappaB (NF-kappaB) pathway (TPCA-1) or TLR2 (C29) were applied in vitro to pinpoint the signaling cascade. Their potential therapeutic effects were further assessed by administration in the UAC model. RESULTS: Clinical samples revealed elevated PF4 levels in the SF of TMJOA patients, correlating with simulated mechanical stress at the condyle. In a rat UAC model, mechanical overload similarly upregulated PF4 in TMJ, concomitant with cartilage degeneration, anabolic-catabolic imbalance, and cellular senescence. In vitro, PF4 stimulation of primary chondrocytes suppressed anabolic markers while upregulating catabolic factors and senescence markers. Mechanistically, PF4 uniquely activated the canonical NF-kappaB pathway by directly engaging surface TLR2, bypassing its classical chemokine receptor C-X-C motif chemokine receptor 3 (CXCR3). This PF4-TLR2 interaction was both necessary and sufficient for downstream NF-kappaB-driven gene dysregulation. Notably, this PF4-TLR2 axis upregulates B-cell CLL/lymphoma 3 (BCL3), which in turn promotes pathway activation by accelerating early phosphorylation of p65, revealing an intrinsic feedback loop that fine-tunes the inflammatory response. In vivo, inhibition of TLR2 or canonical NF-kappaB signaling in the UAC model significantly mitigated overload-induced cartilage dysregulation and subchondral bone damage. CONCLUSION: We delineate a novel mechanotransduction pathway in TMJOA, where overload-induced PF4 acts as an alarmin that signals through TLR2 to activate the canonical NF-kappaB cascade, a process further amplified by the downstream regulator BCL3, ultimately disrupting cartilage homeostasis. This work establishes the PF4-TLR2-NF-kappaB axis as a crucial pathogenic driver and a promising therapeutic target for load-related TMJ degeneration.

title: Integrative Multi-Omics and Experimental Validation Define RELB as an Immune-Related Prognostic Driver in Ovarian Cancer.
authors: Leng, Wenshu; Fan, Xingyue; Fang, Yichen
abstract: Ovarian cancer (OC) is one of the most aggressive gynecological malignancies worldwide. The tumor microenvironment and transcriptomic alterations play important roles in OC progression and therapeutic response. Integrative bulk and single-cell transcriptomic analyses may facilitate the identification of prognostic biomarkers and potential therapeutic targets. Multi-Omic datasets from TCGA and GEO were analyzed. Immune-related genes were first integrated with survival information and screened using a random survival forest model to identify five core genes. GO/KEGG analyses were performed on differentially expressed genes, while GSEA and GSVA were used to characterize pathways associated with the core genes. Single-cell RNA-seq data were processed to determine cell-type-specific expression patterns. Molecular docking predicted potential gene-drug interactions. CCK-8, Transwell, and flow cytometry assays assessed the functional role of RELB in OC cells. Five core genes-RELB, CXCL9, PI3, TRAC, and CXCL11-were identified through integration of immune-related genes and random survival forest analysis. Drug sensitivity analysis showed that the expression of all five genes was associated with sensitivity to KU-55933. High expression of key genes was associated with altered immune-related features, while CXCL9, CXCL11, and TRAC were positively associated with CD8+ T-cell abundance and cytolytic activity. Single-cell sequencing identified seven cell types, among which CXCL9 and CXCL11 were highly expressed in monocytes, TRAC in T cells, and PI3 in epithelial cells. Molecular docking predicted a potential interaction between PI3 and 6atu-PROGESTERONE, with a binding energy of -6.35 kcal/mol. RELB was highly expressed in OC cells, and its knockdown significantly inhibited cell proliferation, migration, and invasion while promoting apoptosis. This study identifies a five-gene prognostic signature linked to the immune microenvironment in ovarian cancer. Among them, RELB showed a functional role in OC cell malignant phenotypes, supporting its potential as a biomarker and therapeutic target. Computational drug sensitivity and docking analyses provide hypothesis-generating evidence for potential therapeutic associations that require experimental validation.

title: A TRIM15-CDX2 loop drives bile acid-induced gastric intestinal metaplasia.
authors: Wang, Dan; Chen, Jian; Xu, Wei; Shrestha, Sachin Mulmi; Lu, Qin; Ren, Lihua; Ji, Qinghua; Wu, Hailu; Shi, Ruihua
abstract: BACKGROUND: Gastric intestinal metaplasia (GIM), a precancerous lesion and risk factor for gastric cancer, is closely associated with chronic bile acid (BA) exposure; however, its molecular mechanisms remain unclear. This study aimed to identify key regulators involved in BA-associated GIM and to elucidate their functional roles. METHODS: TRIM15 and GIM markers (CDX2, MUC2, KLF4, and VIL1) were assessed in human GIM and paired normal tissues by RNA-seq, RT‒qPCR, Western blotting (WB), and immunofluorescence (IF). BA profiles were analyzed using UHPLC‒MS/MS. In vitro, GES-1 cells were treated with CDCA and subjected to TRIM15 gain- and loss-of-function assays. CDX2-mediated transcriptional regulation of TRIM15 was evaluated by dual-luciferase reporter and ChIP assays. NF-kappaB signaling and related proteins were assessed by WB and IF. The interaction between TRIM15 and IkappaBalpha and the levels of ubiquitination were investigated by coimmunoprecipitation, LC-MS/MS and protein-protein docking analysis. Functional assays were used to assess proliferation and apoptosis. In vivo validation was performed using an AAV9-mediated TRIM15 knockdown rat model. RESULTS: TRIM15 expression was consistently upregulated in GIM and increased stepwise with disease severity, accompanied by a positive association with CDX2 expression. BA profiling revealed the selective enrichment of cholic acid (CA) and chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA), which induced GIM-associated phenotypes in vitro. Mechanistically, CDX2 directly bound to the TRIM15 promoter to increase its transcription, whereas TRIM15 promoted CDX2 expression via the NF-kappaB pathway, resulting in the formation of a regulatory loop. Further mechanistic analyses revealed that TRIM15 promoted K48-linked ubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation of IkappaBalpha, thereby enhancing p65 phosphorylation. Notably, this effect was abolished by expression of the degradation-resistant IkappaBalpha S32A/S36A mutant. In vivo, TRIM15 knockdown attenuated gastric mucosal injury and intestinal metaplasia and reduced NF-kappaB signaling and CDX2 expression. CONCLUSION: These findings suggest the involvement of a TRIM15-NF-kappaB-CDX2 regulatory loop in BA-associated GIM. TRIM15 may contribute to epithelial reprogramming under BA exposure and could be a potential biomarker and therapeutic target for GIM progression.

title: [Ergosterol peroxide inhibits proliferation of breast cancer MDA-MB-231 cells via synergistic ferroptosis and mitochondrial-dependent apoptosis mediated by p53 signaling pathway].
authors: Hou, Li-Man; Luo, Ran; Wang, Qi; Wang, Lu; Deng, Si-Qi; Bu, Ming; Lin, Yu
journal: Zhongguo Zhong yao za zhi = Zhongguo zhongyao zazhi = China journal of Chinese materia medica
abstract: Based on proteomic methods, this paper aims to explore the target and action mechanism of ergosterol peroxide(EP) against triple-negative breast cancer. The effect of EP on the viability of breast cancer MDA-MB-231 cells was detected by the MTT method. The effect of EP on apoptosis, mitochondrial membrane potential(detected by JC-1), reactive oxygen species(ROS), and the cell cycle of MDA-MB-231 cells was detected by flow cytometry. The subcellular localization and differentially expressed proteins of MDA-MB-231 cells treated with EP were obtained by proteomic technology based on tandem mass spectrometry. GO function and KEGG enrichment analysis were conducted through the eggNOG and KAAS databases. A protein-protein interaction(PPI) network was constructed via the STRING database. Malondialdehyde(MDA), superoxide dismutase(SOD), and glutathione(GSH) concentrations, as well as iron contents, were measured using a microplate reader. A Western blot was performed to detect the expression of relevant proteins, and molecular docking was used to validate the binding affinity of EP to relevant core target proteins. MTT results demonstrate that EP significantly inhibits MDA-MB-231 cell viability in a time-and concentration-dependent manner. The results of flow cytometry show that after MDA-MB-231 cells are treated with EP of 10, 20, and 40 mumol.L~(-1) for 48 hours, the total apoptosis rate of the cells increases significantly. The mitochondrial membrane potential decreased significantly; the level of ROS increased significantly; cell cycle arrest occurred in the G_0/G_1 phase. Proteomic results demonstrate that compared with those in the blank group, 895 differentially expressed proteins are identified in the EP group, with 326 upregulated proteins and 569 downregulated proteins. Bioinformatics pathway enrichment analysis indicates significant enrichment of ferroptosis and tumor protein p53 signaling pathways among these differentially expressed proteins, suggesting that EP may exert an inhibitory effect on MDA-MB-231 cell proliferation through multiple pathways. The Western blot results show that the protein expressions of cytochrome C(Cyt C), B-cell lymphoma-2(Bcl-2)-associated X protein(Bax), cleaved cysteine-aspartic acid protease-7(cleaved caspase-7), heme oxygenase 1(HOMX1), p53, and p21 protein are increased in MDA-MB-231 cells treated with EP.
