In contrast, the protein expressions of Bcl-2, solute carrier family 7 member 11(SLC7A11), glutathione peroxidase 4(GPX4), regulatory subunit of glutamate-cysteine ligase(GCLM), p62 protein, and cyclin-dependent kinase 4(CDK4) are decreased. The above findings suggest that EP may promote apoptosis in MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cells by regulating the p53 signaling pathway and inducing ferroptosis.

title: [Compound Danshen Cataplasm promoting acclimatization to high-altitude environments].
authors: Chen, Yu-Ting; Niu, Hong; Wang, Jing-Zhe; Li, Meng-Zhen; Guo, Jin; Jin, Yi-Guang; DU, Li-Na
journal: Zhongguo Zhong yao za zhi = Zhongguo zhongyao zazhi = China journal of Chinese materia medica
abstract: To address acute mountain sickness(AMS) easily induced by low pressure, hypoxia, and intense ultraviolet radiation in high-altitude environments, a novel Compound Danshen Cataplasm(CDC) was developed, and its adhesive properties were evaluated. The hippocampal neuron(HT22) hypoxia model and small-animal hypoxia model were established. The anti-hypoxia and anti-AMS efficacy of CDC was assessed by an open field test, novel object recognition test, routine blood examination, sleep duration measurement, determination of brain and lung wet-to-dry ratios, detection of inflammatory and oxidative stress factors, and pathological section observation. In addition, network pharmacology and molecular docking simulations were employed to explore the underlying mechanism of action. The results show that CDC can significantly increase the survival rate of HT22 cells under hypoxia, reduce cell apoptosis, improve spontaneous exploration ability and cognitive function of hypoxic model mice, prolong sleep duration under hypoxic conditions, promote blood cell recovery, alleviate brain and lung edema, significantly reduce the levels of TNF-alpha, i NOS, IL-6, and MDA in blood, brain tissue, and lung tissue of mice, increase SOD activity(P<0. 01), and markedly alleviate hypoxia-induced brain and lung edema as well as inflammatory cell infiltration. Network pharmacology results reveal that the binding energies between key active components of CDC and core disease targets are all less than-5 k J.mol~(-1), and that CDC can downregulate the protein expression levels of relevant genes STAT3, JAK1, JAK2, and their phosphorylated forms in the brain tissue of mice. In conclusion, CDC can meet the need for prolonged efficacy under urgent and special conditions, demonstrating significant potential application value.

title: MaltEms-MaltOBP9 axis mediates sexually dimorphic olfactory behavior in Monochamus alternatus via recognition of pheromone 2-methoxy-4-vinylphenol.
authors: Yang, Mei-Jiao; Sun, Wei; Li, Qi-Cheng; Wei, Yan-Lin; Zhang, Pu-Yuan; Gu, Jian; Wang, Man-Qun
abstract: The olfactory system is essential for insect survival and behavior, with odorant-binding proteins (OBPs) playing a key role by binding and transporting chemical signals to olfactory receptors. Although MaltOBP9 from Monochamus alternatus, a primary vector of pine wilt disease, has been linked to olfactory functions in M. alternatus, its regulatory mechanisms and specific roles are not well understood. In this study, we show that MaltOBP9 is highly expressed in the antennae of both male and female adults after sexual maturation. Using fluorescence spectroscopy, molecular docking, and site-directed mutagenesis, we identified the amino acid Phe54 as essential for MaltOBP9's ability to bind 18 different volatile compounds. RNA interference (RNAi) and behavioral tests revealed that MaltOBP9 is necessary for sexually mature adults to detect the pheromone 2-methoxy-4-vinylphenol (2M4VP). Additionally, dual-luciferase reporter assays, electrophoretic mobility shift assays, and RNAi experiments demonstrated that the transcription factor MaltEms positively regulates MaltOBP9 expression, thereby influencing the detection of 2M4VP. By combining insights into transcriptional regulation and protein-ligand interactions, this study clarifies the MaltEms-MaltOBP9-2M4VP axis as a mediator of sex-specific olfactory behavior-where females avoid and males are attracted to the pheromone-in sexually mature M. alternatus. These findings provide a theoretical basis for developing pest control methods that target MaltOBP9 and its critical residue Phe54 through behavior-based strategies.

title: Structural mechanism of TRPC3 inhibition by a potent antagonist.
authors: Collingridge, Jodie; Cole, Bethan A; Rowlett, Molly A; Liddle, John; Gatfield, Kelly M; Biggin, Philip C; Becker, Ebe
abstract: The transient receptor channel canonical family member 3 (TRPC3) is a non-selective, calcium-permeable cation channel within the larger TRP superfamily. TRPC3 is expressed in both excitable and non-excitable cells, where it integrates multiple signaling pathways and is directly activated by binding of diacylglycerol following activation of G-protein coupled receptors. Increased TRPC3 signaling is implicated in several diseases, highlighting TRPC3 as a potential therapeutic target. However, the development of TRPC3 inhibitors with suitable potency and selectivity has been challenging due to the channel's high structural and sequence homology with related family members, specifically TRPC6. Here, we present a highly potent TRPC3 antagonist (GSK2820986A) featuring an anilino-thiazole pharmacophore. Through a combination of molecular dynamic simulations and functional assays, we identify a putative binding site for GSK2820986A in the S4-S5 pocket and propose a potential inhibitory mechanism. Our findings provide a powerful tool compound and mechanistic framework to advance the investigation and therapeutic targeting of TRPC3.

title: Gut-Mitophagy-Ferroptosis Axis in Asthma: Microvirga-TP53-PARP11 Crosstalk as a Quantifiable Target for Childhood Asthma Prevention.
authors: Sun, Teng; Bi, Junjie; Zhang, Jingjing; Ye, Lei
journal: Critical reviews in eukaryotic gene expression
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Asthma affects over 260 million individuals globally; however, its heterogeneous subtypes pose significant challenges to precision prevention. Although gut microbiome dysbiosis and mitophagy and ferroptosis dysfunction have been implicated in asthma pathogenesis, the potential causal interactions between these pathways remain unclear. METHODS: We performed two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) to assess the causal effects of 473 gut microbial taxa and 49 mitophagy-related genes on four distinct asthma subtypes. Mediation and reverse MR analyses were further employed to explore potential mitophagy-mediated pathways and assess feedback effects from asthma liability on the gut microbiota. For the mitophagy-related mediator genes, we further dissected the ferroptotic pathway-mediated downstream mechanisms and performed drug candidate enrichment and molecular docking. RESULTS: MR analysis identified 20, 19, 13, and 15 gut bacterial taxa that were causally associated with non-allergic, allergic, childhood, and eosinophilic asthma, respectively. Four mitophagy-related genes TP53, MAP1LC3A, NBR1, and CSNK2B exhibited subtype-specific associations. Mediation analysis suggested that TP53-mediated mitophagy mediates 7.7% of the total effect of Microvirga against childhood asthma. Approximately 49% of the total protective effect of TP53 was partially offset through its down-regulation of PARP11-mediated ferroptosis. DSigDB-selected baicalin and theaflavin both stably docked to TP53 at 7.8 kcal mol-1, which offers natural origin, low toxicity, and high affinity. CONCLUSION: Our findings support the existence of a gut-mitophagy-ferroptosis-lung axis in asthma pathogenesis. Notably, the Microvirga-TP53-PARP11axis demonstrates a quantifiable protective association with childhood asthma. These insights highlight a potential opportunity for precision, subtype-specific prevention strategies targeting this pathway in early life.

title: Exploration of Potential Molecular Mechanisms and Key Genes Related to T-Cell Exhaustion in Coronary Heart Disease from a Bioinformatics Perspective.
authors: Liu, Fei; Liu, Wen; Zhang, Zhiliang; Peng, Xiaoping; Wen, Yuan
journal: Critical reviews in eukaryotic gene expression
abstract: Coronary heart disease (CHD), a major cardiovascular disorder, is associated with T cell exhaustion (TEX) in its pathogenesis. This study aimed to identify TEX-related key genes in CHD and explore their potential mechanisms. The training set, validation set, and TEX-related genes (TEX-RGs) were downloaded from public databases. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified and intersected with TEX-RGs to obtain candidate genes. LASSO regression and Wilcoxon rank-sum test were then used to screen key genes. A nomogram for CHD prediction was constructed and validated via calibration curves and ROC curves. Finally, analyses related to functional enrichment, cell infiltration, T cell state score (TCSS) evaluation, regulatory network construction, drug prediction, and molecular docking were performed for key genes. Initially, the 48 candidate genes were identified, followed by the determination of two key genes (BST2 and XPC). A nomogram integrating BST2 and XPC showed high prediction performance. Functional enrichment analysis indicated their involvement in oxidative phosphorylation, spliceosome, and other processes. Notably, CHD patients exhibited altered infiltration of CD8+ effector memory T cells and chondrocytes, with imbalanced TCSS in Quiescence and Terminal Exhaustion T cell subsets. Regulatory network analysis identified transcription factors (e.g., GATA1, and SP1), microRNAs (e.g., hsa-miR-942-5p), and long non-coding RNAs (e.g., H19) associated with key genes. Potential drugs interacting with key genes (e.g., alvespimycin, MG-262) were predicted, though molecular docking revealed weak binding ability. Collectively, these findings provided valuable insights into the molecular mechanisms of CHD, offering a theoretical basis for understanding the disease and developing targeted therapeutic strategies.

title: Quantifying the impact of genetic mutations on enhancer dynamics.
authors: Das, Maitreya; Banerjee, Deepro; Hossain, Ayaan; Jensen, Matthew; Mogre, Saie; Sun, Jiawan; Mao, Joseph; Glick, Adam B; Salis, Howard M; Girirajan, Santhosh
abstract: Transcriptional regulation is mediated by enhancers, yet how genetic perturbations alter enhancer activity and gene expression remains unclear. We develop UDI-UMI-STARR-seq, integrating dual indexes and unique molecular identifiers, and combine it with RNA-seq to profile perturbation-associated changes in enhancer activity and gene expression. We apply this approach to 253,632 fragments representing 46,142 cell type-specific candidate enhancers and assess the impact of CRISPR/Cas9-mediated deletion of six transcription factors (ATF2, CTCF, FOXA1, LEF1, TCF7L2, and SCRT1). We identify responsive fragments that are repressed or induced and enriched for p53 family motifs. Enhancer-gene mapping reveals associations between responsive fragments and gene expression changes, including Wnt/p53 targets after ATF2 or LEF1 depletion. A deep learning model recapitulates enhancer grammar, including cooperative motif syntax and flanking sequence context. Applying this framework to 16p12.1 deletion identifies responsive fragments associated with genes involved in neuronal function, providing a scalable readout of enhancer dynamics across genetic perturbations.

title: Notoginsenoside R1 modulates the ATF4-CHOP-Bcl2 signaling pathway to alleviate mitochondrial stress damage and apoptosis in asthmatic airway epithelial cells.
authors: Ling, Yaozheng; Guan, Ling; Zhao, Yu; Fu, Zhou; Zou, Wenjing
abstract: OBJECTIVE: To investigate whether Notoginsenoside R1 (NG-R1) improves mitochondrial homeostasis by targeting the integrin signaling response (ISR) core transcription factor ATF4, thereby alleviating damage and apoptosis in asthma airway epithelial cells. METHODS: House dust mites (HDM) were used to establish an in vivo asthma mouse model and an in vitro BEAS-2B cell model. The anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory effects of NG-R1 were evaluated through pulmonary function testing, bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) cell counting, and hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining. We evaluated the effects of NG-R1 on apoptosis and mitochondrial function using TUNEL, Annexin V-FITC/PI staining, transmission electron microscopy, MitoSox Red, TMRE, JC-1, and Western blot analysis of mitochondrial dynamics-related proteins (p-Drp1/Drp1, Mfn2, ATP5F1A). We used lentiviral knockdown of ATF4 combined with RNA-seq, GO enrichment analysis, and the STRING database to predict its downstream mechanisms. Molecular docking was used to predict the binding affinity between NG-R1 and ATF4, and the expression levels of ATF4, CHOP, and Bcl-2 were validated using Western blot analysis in both in vivo and in vitro models. RESULTS: ATF4 expression was significantly elevated in lung tissue from asthmatic mice and in HDM-stimulated BEAS-2B cells, and was positively correlated with increased epithelial cell apoptosis and reduced migration and repair capacity. ATF4 knockdown alleviates HDM-induced increases in mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS), decreases in membrane potential, mitochondrial ultrastructural damage, and disbalance in fission/fusion (downregulation of p-Drp1/Drp1 and upregulation of Mfn2 and ATP5F1A) via the ATF4-CHOP-Bcl2 signaling pathway, thereby inhibiting apoptosis. NG-R1 intervention significantly reduced airway hyperresponsiveness, total inflammatory cell counts in BALF, and levels of Th2 cytokines (IL-4, IL-13, IL-33) in asthmatic mice, and alleviated pulmonary inflammatory infiltration. Molecular docking and in vitro and in vivo experiments indicated that NG-R1 may specifically downregulate ATF4 (binding energies of -5.761 and -6.553 kcal/mol, respectively), modulate CHOP-Bcl2 expression levels, improve mitochondrial function and dynamic equilibrium, inhibit epithelial cell apoptosis, and promote migration and repair. CONCLUSION: NG-R1 may regulate the ATF4-CHOP-Bcl2 signaling pathway by specifically binding to and downregulating ATF4, thereby alleviating mitochondrial stress-induced damage, inhibiting airway epithelial cell apoptosis, and promoting epithelial repair, suggesting that NG-R1 is a potential candidate drug for targeted asthma therapy.

title: Selective behavioral and prefrontal transcriptomic correlates of acute clozapine exposure in socially isolated mice.
authors: Xu, Youzhi; Gao, Ao; Zhang, Yixuan; Zhang, Zishen; Zhao, Yanzhi; Huo, Chunyue
abstract: BACKGROUND: Clozapine is an effective antipsychotic for treatment-resistant schizophrenia, but acute molecular responses to clozapine remain incompletely characterized. Social isolation rearing produces schizophrenia-relevant behavioral abnormalities and permits joint evaluation of housing and drug exposure. OBJECTIVE: To characterize behavioral and prefrontal transcriptomic correlates of an acute clozapine challenge in socially isolated mice, reassess previously prioritized Ank3 and Nrxn1, and provide external cellular-context hypotheses for candidate genes. METHODS: Male C57BL/6J mice were evaluated in a four-group housing-by-drug design using open-field, novel-object recognition and prepulse-inhibition tests. For a reproducible transcriptome-wide audit, 11 publicly retrievable prefrontal cortex libraries were re-quantified using a factorial DESeq2 model with false-discovery-rate control. Historical pairwise prioritization, network analysis, machine-learning screening, molecular docking and molecular-dynamics simulations were treated as exploratory analyses. Adult wild-type prefrontal cortex single-cell RNA-seq data were used for cellular localization, CellChat analysis and virtual knockout, whereas an embryonic cortical reference was used separately for CellOracle transcription-factor perturbation. RESULTS: Acute clozapine showed its clearest behavioral effect on isolation-associated hyperlocomotion, whereas recognition memory was not improved and prepulse-inhibition results varied by stimulus intensity. The primary DESeq2 analysis identified 56 housing-by-drug interaction genes at FDR <0.05; Lamb2 was the strongest FDR-supported transcriptomic signal. Nrxn1 showed directionally opposite changes in historical pairwise contrasts but did not reach FDR significance in the factorial model, whereas Ank3 showed no corresponding factorial support. In adult prefrontal cortex single-cell data, Lamb2 was concentrated in endothelial cells, while Ank3 and Nrxn1 were broadly detected in neuronal populations. Virtual Ank3 and Nrxn1 knockout profiles contained 16 and 15 significant non-target genes, respectively, with five shared genes and no significant reciprocal candidate effect. Embryonic CellOracle analyses identified model-dependent upstream transcription-factor sensitivity of Ank3 and Nrxn1. CONCLUSION: These findings define selective behavioral and prefrontal transcriptomic correlates of an acute clozapine challenge rather than generalized behavioral rescue or clinical treatment-response prediction. Lamb2 was the strongest FDR-supported signal in the primary model, whereas Ank3 and Nrxn1 remain exploratory computational candidates. The external single-cell and virtual-perturbation analyses provide testable cellular and regulatory hypotheses, not evidence of direct binding, causal regulation or clozapine-induced effects in vivo.

title: Machine learning-guided leaf margin classification and discovery that BcPHB promoter selection rewires a BcPHB-BcLMI1 module to shape leaf margins in Brassica campestris.
authors: Chen, Jingwen; Li, Airong; Wu, Tianqi; Huang, Zhenyu; Li, Xiyao; Xu, Shan; Wu, Yujie; Tian, Yuan; Chen, Weiwei; Quan, Xinhua; Yao, Xiangtan; Lin, Sue; Feng, Xuping; Huang, Li
abstract: The morphological diversification of leaf margins reflects the evolutionary reshaping of conserved developmental programs. However, fully deciphering the underlying molecular basis remains challenging due to difficulties in phenotype quantification and the incomplete characterization of complex regulatory networks. In this study, we established a computer-vision framework to decode leaf lobe trait and identified the HD-ZIP III factor PHABULOSA (BcPHB), combining genome-wide association studies (GWAS) and selective sweep analysis in Brassica campestris. We found that promoter variation defines two major haplotypes, BcPHB(HapI) and BcPHB(HapII), driving divergent expression levels associated with entire and lobed leaves. Functionally, BcPHB knockdown lines (BcPHB(ami)) exhibited lobed margins, whereas complementation of lobed accessions with the BcPHB(HapI) promoter partially restored the entire-leaf phenotype. Similarly, overexpression of LATE MERISTEM IDENTITY 1 (BcLMI1), a conserved regulator of leaf lobation, phenocopied the BcPHB(ami) lines. Mechanistically, BcPHB and BcLMI1 form a reciprocal negative feedback loop that stabilizes margin patterning. Furthermore, domestication-driven selection of BcPHB(HapI) facilitated the transition from ancestral lobed leaves to cultivated entire forms. This study reveals a pivotal developmental module and illustrates how regulatory evolution drives morphological diversification in crops.

title: Understanding cell fate decisions with temporal attention.
authors: Burger, Florian; Dias Gomes, Martim; Granada, Adrian E; Moreau, Noemie; Bozek, Katarzyna
abstract: Understanding non-genetic determinants of cell fate is critical for developing and improving cancer therapies, as genetically identical cells can exhibit divergent outcomes under the same treatment conditions. In this work, we present a deep learning approach for cell fate prediction from raw long-term live-cell recordings of cancer cell populations under chemotherapeutic treatment. Our Transformer model is trained to predict cell fate directly from raw image sequences, without relying on predefined morphological or molecular features. Beyond classification, we introduce a comprehensive explainability framework for interpreting the temporal and morphological cues guiding the model's predictions. We demonstrate that prediction of cell outcomes is possible based on the video only, our model achieves balanced accuracy of 0.94 and an F1-score of 0.93. Attention and masking experiments further indicate that the signal predictive of the cell fate is not uniquely located in the final frames of a cell trajectory, as reliable predictions are possible up to 8 h before the event. Our analysis reveals distinct temporal distribution of predictive information in the mitotic and apoptotic sequences, as well as the role of cell morphology and p53 signaling in determining cell outcomes. Together, these findings demonstrate that attention-based temporal models enable accurate cell fate prediction while providing biologically interpretable insights into non-genetic determinants of cellular decision-making.

title: Study of the Mechanism of Xianglian Anchang Decoction Ameliorating Ulcerative Colitis Based on Transcriptomics and Network Pharmacology Analysis.
authors: Gao, Tianyu; Zhao, Cuimei; Lu, Lishan; Luo, Ziyue; Wang, Chen; Ma, Junzhuo; Ren, Xuetong; Xu, Xiaosong; Chen, Jiong; Lv, Jingjing; Zhang, Shixiong; Yang, Qian; Wang, Yangang
abstract: INTRODUCTION: The therapeutic efficacy of Xianglian Anchang Decoction (XLAC) in Ulcerative Colitis (UC) has been established, but the underlying pharmacological mechanisms have remained poorly elucidated. In this study, we employed an integrated strategy combining network pharmacology, transcriptomic profiling, and in vivo experimentation to reveal these mechanisms, with a particular focus on how XLAC modulates the IL-17/AP-1 signaling axis to attenuate intestinal inflammation and promote mucosal repair. METHODS: UC was induced in mice by 2% Dextran Sulfate Sodium (DSS) administration in drinking water. The animals were randomly divided into five groups: control (untreated), model (DSS only), XLAC-L (12.4 g/kg/day XLAC extract), XLAC-H (24.8 g/kg/day XLAC extract), and sulfasalazine reference (SASP) (5 g/kg/day sulfasalazine reference drug). Following a 7-day treatment period, various parameters were evaluated, including body mass fluctuations, colon dimensions, microscopic tissue alterations, and intestinal barrier integrity biomarker levels. A computational target prediction analysis was performed to elucidate the pharmacological mechanisms of XLAC, with subsequent transcriptome sequencing verification. Analytical techniques including fluorescence-activated cell sorting, protein immunoblotting, and tissue staining were employed to investigate the modulatory impact of XLAC on UC via the IL-17/AP-1 molecular cascade. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations were performed to evaluate constituent-target binding and complex stability. RESULTS: XLAC significantly prevented DSS-induced body weight loss, preserved colon length, and reduced the severity of colonic histopathological injury. The XLAC intervention suppressed the secretion of inflammatory mediators such as IL-6 and TNF-alpha, while concurrently promoting the expression of the tight junctional protein ZO-1. Integrated network pharmacology and transcriptomic profiling identified the IL-17 signaling pathway as a potential mechanism underlying the therapeutic effect of XLAC against UC. Further experiments validated that XLAC decreased IL-17A levels and inhibited both the expression and phosphorylation of the AP-1 transcription factors c-Jun and c-Fos. Molecular docking revealed stable binding between the principal bioactive constituents of XLAC (beta-sitosterol and quercetin) and the c-Jun/c-Fos protein complex. Molecular dynamics simulations demonstrate the structural stability of the beta-sitosterol-c-FOS complex. DISCUSSION: Our findings reveal a critical role of the IL‑17/AP‑1 signaling axis in the pathogenesis of Ulcerative Colitis (UC) and demonstrate that XLAC may exert its therapeutic effects through this pathway. The multi‑target regulatory mechanism of XLAC provides a molecular basis for its superior efficacy and fewer side effects compared with conventional single‑target therapies. These data support the potential of XLAC as a candidate drug for UC treatment. CONCLUSION: XLAC exerted protective effects against UC by regulating the IL-17/AP-1 signaling pathway, suppressing the inflammatory responses, and promoting intestinal mucosal barrier repair. These findings provide a mechanistic basis that supports the clinical application of XLAC in UC treatment.

title: Esmolol Alleviates Sepsis-Associated Myocardial Injury by Acting on the APAF1 and JAK2/STAT3 Inflammatory Pathways.
authors: Zhao, Lei; Dong, Hua; Dong, Shimin
abstract: OBJECTIVE: The aim of this study is to explore the protective effect of esmolol against sepsis-associated myocardial injury (SAMI) and its underlying molecular mechanisms. METHODS: SAMI-related differentially expressed genes were identified from the Gene Expression Omnibus database (GSE267388). Potential targets of esmolol were predicted using PharmMapper. Overlapping genes were used for enrichment and molecular docking analyses. H9C2 cells were treated with LPS to establish an injury model, followed by esmolol treatment. Cell viability, apoptosis, oxidative stress, and mitochondrial function were also assessed. The expressions of apoptotic protease activating factor 1 (APAF1) and JAK2/STAT3 pathway molecules were detected using reverse transcription-quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) and Western blotting. A rat model of sepsis was used to verify cardiac function, inflammation, oxidative stress, and related protein expression. RESULTS: Six core targets were screened, and esmolol showed the strongest binding to APAF1. Esmolol increased cell viability; reduced apoptosis, ROS, and MDA; restored mitochondrial membrane potential; downregulated APAF1, Bax, cleaved-caspase-9/3; and suppressed JAK2/STAT3 phosphorylation. Esmolol reversed APAF1 overexpression-induced injury. In vivo, esmolol alleviated myocardial pathological injury, decreased the concentrations of myocardial markers and inflammatory factors, and inhibited the APAF1 and JAK2/STAT3 pathways. CONCLUSION: Esmolol protects against SAMI by dual inhibition of the APAF1 mitochondrial apoptotic and JAK2/STAT3 inflammatory pathways, with APAF1 likely serving as a key downstream target of esmolol.

title: Neurotensin modulation of immune and oxido-inflammatory homeostasis targeting TGF-beta activated kinase 1/Nuclear factor-kappa betaeta pathway: an integrated in vivo and in silico study.
authors: Mishra, Swarnima; Mohanty, Banalata
journal: Daru : journal of Faculty of Pharmacy, Tehran University of Medical Sciences
abstract: BACKGROUND: Neurotensin (NTS) is a brain peptide and is known to regulate several brain pathways. Subsequently NTS involvement in psychosis was administered having its promising therapeutic effects as an antipsychotic drug. Therefore, it has been deduced that targeting the NTS system in the regulation of the immune organs would prove to be a productive strategy for developing the novel immune modulatory drugs. OBJECTIVE: The present study elucidated the potential anti-inflammatory properties of NTS receptor 1 (NTSR1) agonist PD149163 (PD) in modulation of immune organs specifically, spleen and thymus investigating the potential immunomodulatory mechanisms targeting NF-kappaB /TAK1 signaling pathway. METHODS: Swiss albino female mice were randomly grouped: Group I-control, treatment groups- Group II, Group III and Group IV were intraperitoneally exposed with NTSR1-agonist PD low dose/ PD(50) (50 microg /kg bw), PD high dose/ PD(100) (100 microg /kg bw) and NTSR1-antagonist SR48692 (500 microg /kg bw), respectively for 28 days. Biochemical, hematological, histopathological, and bioinformatics analyses were performed. Differences were considered statistically significant at P < 0.05. RESULTS: The levels of Nuclear factor kappa beta/NF-kappaB, Tumor necrosis factor- alpha/TNF-alpha, Interleukine-6/IL-6, Corticosterone/CORT and pro-oxidant, Lipid-peroxidation/LPx were visibly similar to control after the treatment of PD(100) as well as PD(50) dose however the elevation was observed with the SR. PD(100) dose has a prominent effect on the plasma Interleukine-10/IL-10, CORT, NTS levels and tissue anti-oxidants superoxide dismutase/SOD, catalase/CAT as well as positively regulated the hematological and histological parameters, clearly deciphering NTS's immunomodulatory effects. Furthermore, in silico molecular docking analyses showed that PD exhibited high binding affinity with TGF-beta activated kinase 1/TAK1 inflammatory protein, indicating inhibition of TAK1/NF-kappaB downstream signaling pathways. CONCLUSION: NTS receptor 1 analogs might provide a better understanding of the mechanisms by which NTS regulates immune-system and could be further exploited for managing various immune-related disorders.

title: Mechanistic interpretability of a plant genomic foundation model: Data probes, causal interventions, and motif-grounded features.
authors: Kendiukhov, Ihor
abstract: Foundation models trained on plant DNA are increasingly used across plant-biology pipelines, yet their internal representations remain opaque, and existing interpretability claims - based on attention visualization, small synthetic evaluations, or single-number benchmark gains - are vulnerable to GC-content and composition confounds. I present a reproducible, composition-controlled protocol for interpreting plant genomic foundation models: six annotated, chromosome-split benchmarks (80,000 windows) together with GC-matched, realistic-negative and repeat-masked variants of them, learned-from-scratch baselines, phylogenetic residualization, sparse autoencoders tested against JASPAR/PlantTFDB motifs, and per-component causal interventions. It is developed on Plant-DnaGemma and re-run, in its probing, control, sparse-autoencoder and block-ablation stages, on Plant DNABERT and AgroNT. Plant-DnaGemma exceeds a 4-mer logistic baseline by 12 percentage points and a DanQ-style convolutional network by 8 on 5-way region-type classification, but merely ties task-supervised convolutional networks on the binary transcription-start-site and promoter tasks. Against a random background almost every sparse-autoencoder feature matches some plant transcription-factor motif, which shows chiefly that such a background is too weak a control; against a dinucleotide-composition-matched background only four in five (245 of 299) retain a specific motif preference. Species classification reaches 67.5% on a GC-matched four-species subset (25% chance) and region discrimination survives repeat-masking, so those signals are not composition artefacts - but across twelve angiosperms, representational distance correlates with divergence time only because it correlates twice as strongly with GC, and the phylogenetic correlation is zero once GC is residualized out. Per-component ablations indicate that no individual attention head is necessary for the splice-site signal, whereas zeroing a single early-middle feed-forward block can cost a quarter of the classifier's accuracy; at whole-block resolution attention and feed-forward blocks contribute comparably, so the redundancy sits within the attention block rather than across it. The protocol is designed to be model-agnostic and is demonstrated here on three plant genomic foundation models.

title: Novel antioxidant peptides targeting the Keap1-Nrf2 pathway discovered from Ginkgo biloba seeds protein hydrolysate: Combining virtual screening, quantum chemical calculation, and zebrafish models in vivo validation.
authors: Yao, Mengru; Zhang, Yuhao; Yang, Caijing; Li, Tong; Liu, Haiyi; Zhao, Yiyun; Memtimin, Metsawur; Guo, Sheng; Duan, Jin-Ao; Xiao, Ping
abstract: The development of safe, edible, and highly stable food-derived natural antioxidant peptides holds significant practical value for functional foods and dietary health management. Ginkgo biloba seeds (GBS), as a food resource rich in protein, are an ideal raw material for the preparation of food-grade antioxidant peptides. This study uses papain to hydrolyze Ginkgo biloba seeds protein (GBSP). Two novel peptides (LTGMAFR and IGINGFGR, LR-7 and IR-8) were first identified via peptidomics combined with computational approaches. Molecular docking revealed that the selected peptides all exhibit strong binding affinity to Keap1 (-7.8 to -8.2 kcal/mol), surpassing the positive ligand (9-mer Nrf2, -7.2 kcal/mol). Molecular dynamics simulations validated the complex's dynamic stability. Molecular orbital calculations and Fukui function analysis confirm that these two peptides exhibit excellent electron-donating properties. Furthermore, IR-8 exhibits stronger DPPH and ABTS scavenging activities than LR-7. In an H(2)O(2)-induced oxidative stress model in zebrafish, the target peptides reduced ROS and MDA levels in zebrafish larvae, upregulated antioxidant enzyme levels and the mRNA levels of genes downstream of the Nrf2 pathway, and effectively alleviated H(2)O(2)-induced oxidative damage. Western blot results further confirmed that H(2)O(2)-induced oxidative stress reduces nuclear Nrf2 protein levels and the Nrf2 nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, while peptide intervention effectively restores Nrf2 nuclear accumulation. The Nrf2-specific inhibitor ML385 experiments further confirmed that the antioxidant activity of the target peptides depends on the activation of the Nrf2 pathway. This work elucidates the antioxidant mechanism of GBSP targeting the Keap1-Nrf2 pathway and provides an efficient multi-method strategy for natural antioxidant screening.

title: Transcription factor CTCF activates KIAA1199 expression to inhibit ferroptosis and promote malignant behaviors in colorectal cancer based on bioinformatics and machine learning.
authors: Fan, Xiaoye; Meng, Lei; Zheng, Song; He, Xiaoqing
abstract: OBJECTIVES: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is a common malignancy of the colon and rectum, but its molecular mechanisms remain incompletely understood. METHODS: Gene expression omnibus (GEO) database was used to download CRC-related datasets. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA), least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO), support vector machine (SVM), and random forest (RF) were used to identify key CRC genes. Cell type identification by estimating relative subsets of rna transcripts (CIBERSORT) was used for immune infiltration analysis. Tumor immune estimation resource (TIMER) database was used to assess gene expression across multiple cancers. Human transcription factor target database (hTFtarget) was used to predict regulatory relationships between genes and transcription factors. Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP), dual-luciferase assay, cell transfection, western blot (WB), and reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) were used to detect protein-gene binding, transcriptional activity, gene knockdown and overexpression, protein expression, and mRNA expression. JASPAR database was used to identify transcription factor binding sites. Cells were treated with a BODIPY 581/591 C11 kit to assess intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels. The assay kits were employed to determine the levels of ferrous iron (Fe(2+)), malondialdehyde (MDA), and superoxide dismutase (SOD). Cell counting kit-8 (CCK-8) was performed to measure cell viability. RESULTS: Matrix metallopeptidase 7 (MMP7), KIAA1199, and cadherin 3 (CDH3) were identified as potential key CRC genes. Their expression correlated with altered immune cell infiltration patterns. KIAA1199 showed the highest upregulation in CRC tissues. CCCTC-binding factor (CTCF) transcriptionally activated KIAA1199. Knockdown of CTCF decreased the expression of solute carrier family 7 member 11 (SLC7A11) and glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4), while increasing ROS, Fe(2+), and MDA, and decreasing SOD levels. CTCF knockdown combined with KIAA1199 overexpression partially rescued these effects, modulating ferroptosis-related oxidative stress in CRC cells. CONCLUSION: CTCF transcriptionally activates KIAA1199 and regulates ferroptosis-related oxidative stress in CRC cells, providing new insights into the molecular mechanisms of CRC.

title: KRT14 activated by transcription factor E2F1 promotes bladder cancer progression.
authors: Chen, Xingheng; Liu, Sinan; Zhang, Xiaosong; Chen, Xiang; Wang, Chenlu
abstract: Bladder cancer is one of the most common cancers in the world, and its high malignancy threatens human health. Therefore, it is vital to explore new therapeutic targets for the early diagnosis and prognosis evaluation of bladder cancer. Keratin 14 (KRT14) is the oncogene of numerous cancers, but its role and mechanism in bladder cancer are not completely clear. The present study aimed to assess the molecular mechanism of KRT14 in bladder cancer. Bioinformatics analyses were performed to screen KRT14 as an oncogene in bladder cancer. Moreover, KRT14 small interfering RNA and KRT14 overexpression plasmids were transfected into 5637 and RT4 bladder cancer cells. Subsequently, Transwell, Cell Counting Kit-8 and cell colony formation assays were performed to assess changes in cell phenotype. Finally, bioinformatics analysis was performed to screen for transcription factors of KRT14. The results demonstrated that KRT14 was highly expressed in bladder cancer tissues and cell lines, and its expression was associated with a poor prognosis. KRT14 knockdown suppressed proliferation, migration and invasion of 5637 and RT4 cells, whereas ectopic KRT14 overexpression demonstrated the inverse phenotypic changes. E2F transcription factor 1 (E2F1) is an upstream transcription factor of KRT14 and the effects of KRT14 silencing on 5637 cell migration and invasion were attenuated by E2F1 overexpression. In addition, Gene Set Cancer Analysis, drug sensitivity correlation analysis and molecular docking simulation predicted that afatinib, erlotinib and vandetanib may serve as candidate small molecules with potential binding affinity to KRT14. This provides preliminary clues for developing KRT14-intervening agents for bladder cancer. In conclusion, KRT14 is an oncogenic gene that promotes bladder cancer progression upon transcriptional activation by the upstream transcription factor E2F1. Its high expression is associated with poor prognosis, supporting its potential as a prognostic biomarker and therapeutic target in bladder cancer.

title: Interpretable machine learning coupled to gene regulatory networks uncovers subcircuits underlying cell fate decisions.
authors: Rarani, Zarifeh H; Keshari, Swapnil; Sachan, Akanksha; Saini, Ankur; Pease, Nicholas; Fan, Jingyu; Fu, Alayna; Liu, Yuchen C; Gurkar, Aditi U; Delgoffe, Greg M; Singh, Harinder; Das, Jishnu
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Gene regulatory networks (GRNs) model causal linkages that control cell fate decisions and differentiation transitions. Prioritizing regulatory subnetworks underlying cell state differences is of critical importance, but current methods including those reliant on topological metrics introduce circularity as the metrics prioritizing TFs are computed from the same networks whose assumptions they inherit. Separately, interpretable machine learning methods can identify latent factors (LFs) that discriminate cellular states with formal statistical guarantees but do not model regulatory linkages. Here, we present FOCAL (Factor-Outcome Coupling for Assessment of Linkages), a paradigm to prioritize regulatory subnetworks by coupling state-specific and dynamic GRNs with outcome-supervised LFs learned using interpretable machine learning without reference to network topology. This shifts GRN focus from macroscopic TF nodes to state-specific and dynamic TF-gene linkages. In B and T cells, FOCAL identified GIFs (GRNs coupled to Interpretable latent Factors), prioritized regulatory subnetworks underlying established states as well as transient regulatory episodes preceding them. By coupling LFs learnt from perturbation experiments of lineage-defining TFs, FOCAL identified transcriptional predisposition to alternative fates within progenitor cell populations before overt differentiation. This uncovered a novel NFATC2-IRF8 interplay in activated B cells, that was validated by in-vitro and in-vivo genetic perturbations. The two transcription factors act cooperatively to restrain extrafollicular plasmablast differentiation and promote germinal center B cell fate.

title: Genetic risk and inflammatory signaling converge on cell type-specific regulatory programs in type 1 diabetes.
authors: Wang, Liu; Wei, Zong
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is a complex autoimmune disease characterized by the destruction of insulin-producing pancreatic beta cells. Both genetic susceptibility and epigenetic dysregulation contribute to T1D risk. Recent studies have reported beta-cell dysfunction before disease onset, suggesting that beta-cell-intrinsic mechanisms contribute to pathogenesis. However, the mechanistic link between disease-associated variants and beta-cell dysfunction remains poorly understood. We hypothesized that a subset of T1D-associated variants directly influences cell type-specific candidate cis-regulatory elements (cCREs) by disrupting transcription factor (TF) binding and altering gene expression. To define cell type-specific cCREs in human islets, we integrated publicly available epigenomic datasets, including bulk histone modification profiles and single-cell multiomic data from human pancreatic islets. We combined these data with T1D genome-wide association study (GWAS) variants to identify disease-associated SNPs located within enhancer regions. Using multiomic datasets from PANC-DB, we characterized cell type-specific chromatin accessibility in nondiabetic and T1D islets and identified regulatory regions that may control gene expression in beta cells and other islet cell types. We then applied ChromBPNet, a deep learning model that predicts base-pair-resolution chromatin accessibility from scATAC-seq data, to evaluate how specific variants may alter local regulatory activity. In parallel, we used TF footprinting to nominate TFs likely to bind these variant-containing regions. These analyses identified several T1D-associated SNPs predicted to alter chromatin accessibility at candidate TF binding sites, suggesting mechanisms by which noncoding variants may contribute to beta-cell dysfunction and T1D susceptibility. Our findings link T1D-associated variants to cell type-specific enhancer activity and regulatory pathways and provide candidates for future mechanistic studies.

title: Nucleotide State Regulates Asymmetric Substrate-Binding Protein Docking in a Type II ABC Importer
authors: Alexandra Karagiaridi; Ramon Mendoza Uriarte; Muyuan Chen; Benoit Roux; Heather W Pinkett
abstract: Type II ABC importers rely on substrate-binding proteins (SBP) to capture nutrients and deliver them to membrane-embedded transporters, but how ATP binding and hydrolysis regulate their interactions remains poorly understood. To address these questions, we determined structures of the Type II small-substrate molybdate importer MolBC-A from H. influenzae in distinct nucleotide-bound states, complemented by molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and functional assays. In a nucleotide-free state, the MolA-MolBC interface is remodeled into a more open conformation, whereas ATP and AMP-PNP binding induce asymmetric conformational changes that preserve the MolA Lobe I interface and disrupt contacts with MolA Lobe II, revealing a previously unresolved partially-docked state. In the ADP-bound state, MolA exhibits the greatest conformational heterogeneity with reduced stable engagement that extends across both lobes. Together these findings define a nucleotide-dependent cycle of asymmetric MolA remodeling and reveal distinct contributions of the two SBP lobes in coupling transporter nucleotide state to SBP engagement.

title: LigRNA: High-accuracy prediction of RNA-ligand binding sites via dynamic chemical complementarity and language model encoding
authors: Xin Wang; Heqin Zhu; Hao Li; Ao Chang; Feng Zhang; Haobin Chen; Chenxi Wang; Ke Chen; S Kevin Zhou; Peng Xiong
abstract: RNA-binding small molecules represent a validated therapeutic modality, yet pinpointing their exact RNA binding sites remains critical for mechanistic understanding and drug optimization. Experimental methods, while precise, are costly and low-throughput, necessitating robust computational alternatives. Approaches based on static feature concatenation may overlook input-dependent relationships between RNA residues and ligand functional groups. Here we present LigRNA, a graph neural network framework that predicts RNA-ligand binding sites through joint cross-modal encoding of both molecules. LigRNA integrates structure-guided language model embeddings with physicochemical features-solvent-accessible surface area and secondary structure types, to construct comprehensive RNA representations. Ligands are encoded as attributed molecular graphs via graph attention networks, preserving atom-level chemical topology rather than compressing molecules into fixed fingerprints. A cross-attention mechanism then enables dynamic, ligand-dependent modulation of RNA nucleotide attention, capturing context-specific interaction patterns. Benchmarked on TE9 and TE18 datasets, LigRNA achieves F1 scores of 0.73 and 0.58, improving on GATRsite by 7.4% and 18.4%, respectively. Ablation studies identify the RNA residual encoder as the most consistent contributor across the two benchmarks. The source code is freely available at https://github.com/WillowWang0216/LigRNA.

title: A high-resolution protein-RNA binding atlas for structure-aware interaction prediction and post-transcriptional regulatory modeling
authors: Mehran Karimzadeh; Lisa Fish; Heather Karner; Johannes Linder; Ali Emadi; Aldo Hernandez-Corchado; Fatima Zohra Smaili; Khashayar Ghavami; Edna S. Stewart; David Kelley; Bo Wang; Hamed Shateri Najafabadi; Manuel D. Leonetti; Hani Goodarzi
abstract: RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) control post-transcriptional gene expression by regulating RNA processing, localization, stability, and translation. However, our understanding of RNA regulation remains limited by the resolution, scale, and uniformity of available RBP binding maps. Here we introduce eclair CLIP (ecCLIP), a high-throughput CLIP-seq platform that combines endogenous protein tagging for uniform affinity capture with ligation-free library preparation to generate high-resolution RNA-protein binding profiles. We applied ecCLIP to 67 endogenously tagged RBPs in HEK293T cells, generating a high-quality transcriptome-scale atlas that recovered known binding preferences and captured post-transcriptional regulons linked to RNA half-life. To test the utility of the atlas, we incorporated ecCLIP into Borzuki, a Borzoi-derived sequence-to-function model trained on complementary RNA degradation, expression, CLIP, and Perturb-seq data. Inclusion of ecCLIP data improved RNA half-life prediction and assessment of 3 ′ UTR variant effects on RNA stability, demonstrating that our atlas helps capture RNA dynamics. To directly model the cis-regulatory grammar underlying these RBP-RNA interactions, we developed Pythia, a structure-aware neural network architecture that incorporates context-free grammar-inspired fixed convolutions to explicitly encode RNA base-pairing features. Pythia predicted RBP binding from sequence and structural context and decomposed predictions into sequence-and structure-dependent components. We tested this decomposition for five RBPs using massively parallel reporter CLIP (MPRC) binding assays in cells, using synthetic RNA libraries containing mutations designed to preserve or disrupt predicted RNA structures across nominated binding sites. We used the same MPRC strategy to confirm allele-specific binding effects for variants prioritized by Pythia. Together, ecCLIP and Pythia provide a resource for structure-aware decoding of RNA-protein interaction grammar and interpretation of post-transcriptional regulatory variation.

title: Accelerating Molecular Dynamics with Hydrogen Mass Repartitioning to Prioritize Immunogenic Neoantigens for Cancer Vaccines through Peptide HLA Binding Free Energy Calculations
authors: Diego Alfredo Amaya-Ramirez; Jorge Bruce Florez-Suarez; Juan Diego Mora-Fonseca; Carlos Alberto Parra-Lopez
abstract: Personalized neoantigen based vaccines have progressed from concept to clinical evidence for some of the most aggressive human tumors, yet a key challenge remains: determining which candidates should be prioritized for vaccine inclusion. Public neoantigens, shared across tumor subtypes and patient populations, offer potential as off the shelf candidates for broad spectrum immunotherapy. Candidate selection relies on in silico pipelines that estimate binding; however, binding affinity alone is an imperfect marker of immunogenicity. Molecular dynamics (MD) combined with endpoint free energy methods estimates binding free energy directly from simulated trajectories, and hydrogen mass repartitioning (HMR) mitigates the computational cost of hydrogen involving bond vibrations. This study assessed whether HMR accelerated MD can prioritize immunogenic neoantigens through peptide HLA binding free energy calculations and quantified the trade off between accuracy and computational cost. Ten immunogenic public neoantigens (seven paired with their wild type counterparts and three frameshift neoantigens analyzed as unpaired references) were modeled in complex with their HLA I alleles, built de novo using AlphaFold3 and propagated with a 4 fs HMR time step. Mean binding free energy was computed across ten replicas per complex, and each SNV pair was scored concordant with experimental data when the neoantigen formed a more favorable complex than its wild type. Free energies were recomputed at 100 to 500 ns to identify the shortest trajectory preserving reliable ranking. Free energy calculations reproduced experimental concordance for six of seven SNV pairs and were inconclusive for TP53 R8H. Frameshift neoantigens yielded comparable values. Most complexes retained both peptide termini anchored to the HLA groove throughout, and RMSD and RMSF metrics agreed with one another and with the free energy rankings. The PIK3CA E545K (E11K) pair showed the most distinctive signature: the peptides engaged the groove almost identically over P1 to P8, with the entire difference confined to the C terminal pocket, where loss of the wild type's anchor also disrupted its backbone anchor. This pair showed the largest free energy separation in the panel, and restricting analysis to bound frames confirmed a substantial electrostatic and van der Waals advantage favoring the neoantigen. These findings support HMR accelerated binding free energy MD as a practical refinement step for neoantigen prioritization and its application to assessing public neoantigens for cancer vaccine design.

title: Intrinsically disordered regions influence protein motif usage in Drosophila Ubx and AbdA Hox proteins
authors: Maurel-Zaffran C; Edelstein I; Michel L; Macchi M; Caruso N; Saurin AJ; Levy Y; Graba Y
abstract: Hox proteins are evolutionary conserved transcription factors guiding morphogenesis in all bilaterian animals. Conservation mainly concerns the homeodomain (HD), a helix-turn-helix DNA binding motif and flanking sequences close by. Besides, sequences are poorly conserved and disordered. Here we investigate how poorly conserved Intrinsically Disordered Regions (IDRs) influence Hox protein activity, focusing on a closely related Drosophila Hox pair and using a wide range of in vivo function. Studying Drosophila Ultrabithorax (Ubx) and AbdominalA (AbdA) proteins, we find that conserved protein motifs close to the HD are differently used in Ubx and AbdA. Coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations identify a large set of intra-molecular interactions, notably involving poorly conserved disordered regions upstream and downstream the HD. Swapping these regions in Ubx and AbdA alters protein functions and switches motif dependency in some biological situations. This suggests that IDRs, predicted to mediate large and dynamic sets of intramolecular interactions, influence protein motif usage in a context dependent manner.

title: Representing biological concepts as directions in foundation model embeddings
authors: Shamail A; McWhite CD
abstract:
ABSTRACT

Biological foundation models encode rich information about protein structure, function, and cellular state in high-dimensional embeddings, but accessing specific biological properties typically relies on additional, task-specific prediction models. Here, we show that diverse biological properties can be mapped to interpretable, reusable directions in embedding space. In the Concept Activation Vector (CAV) approach, examples representing a concept are distinguished from a background set using a linear model, and the resulting weight vector defines the CAV for that concept. In protein embeddings, CAVs recover Gene Ontology and Enzyme Commission annotations, localize Pfam domains, reveal novel structural relationships, and capture DNA-binding and protein-interaction interface specificity. In single-cell embeddings, CAVs isolate cancer-associated expression transitions, and gene variation along these axes substantially agrees with conventional differential-expression analysis despite being a distinct computational approach. Together, these results establish concept directions as a common representation, enabling diverse biological features to be compared, localized, and manipulated.

title: The eventful journey of a ligand in and out of the binding site
authors: Alessandro Berselli; Michele Parrinello
abstract: The route a ligand follows to reach and leave a protein binding site typically involves complex molecular mechanisms that shape its efficacy as a biologically active compound. These mechanisms are reflected in the binding and unbinding kinetics, which often predict biological activity better than binding affinity alone, yet their calculation remains a bottleneck in ligand characterization. Here, we propose an approach that combines committor-based enhanced sampling with spectral analysis of the infinitesimal generator to characterize in detail how a ligand reaches the binding site of a protein and is eventually expelled. Applied to the paradigmatic benzamidine (BEN)–trypsin complex and the congeneric para-amino benzamidine (PAB), this framework reveals distinct and multifaceted binding pathways for the two ligands, uncovering a previously uncharacterized BEN binding site that competes with the crystallographic site, while identifying a common rotational bottleneck for unbinding. The computed unbinding free energies closely agree with experimental measurements. The spectral decomposition of the infinitesimal generator provides access to the slow dynamical modes of the system. From the slowest mode, we derive residence times and kinetic rate constants that agree with available experimental data and with independent OPES flooding simulations, while requiring substantially less computational effort. This approach offers a privileged perspective to resolve the complexity of protein–ligand binding-unbinding process, with potential applications to ligand screening and the characterization of multiple binding sites.
